lessons.title: What Is React? Why Use It and How It Works
lessons.description: Learn what React is in easy words, why people use it, and the three big ideas: components, state and the virtual DOM.

content.text: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. A user interface, or UI, is everything a person sees and touches on a screen: buttons, menus, lists, forms and pictures. React was made at Facebook and is now used by thousands of companies, from small shops to very large sites. If you want to build modern websites or apps, learning React is one of the most useful steps you can take.
This first lesson has no hard code. It explains the big ideas in easy words, so every later lesson makes sense. Take your time, because these ideas come back in every lesson.
The problem React solves

Think about a shopping cart on a website. When you add a book, many things must change at the same time: the number on the cart icon, the list of items, the total price and maybe a message that says “Added!”. If you write this with plain JavaScript, you must find each part of the page and change it by hand. Miss one part, and the page shows wrong numbers. As the page grows, this gets messy and slow to fix.

React gives you a different way to think. You do not change the page by hand. Instead, you describe what the page should look like for the data you have right now. When the data changes, React works out what must change on the screen and updates only those parts. You say **what** you want, and React takes care of **how**.
A simple way to remember it: with plain JavaScript you give the browser step-by-step orders. With React you give it a picture of the result, and React makes the screen match the picture.
Big idea 1: components

A **component** is a small, reusable piece of the screen. A button can be a component. A product card can be a component. A whole page can be a component made of smaller ones. You build a page the way you build with building blocks: small pieces joined into bigger pieces.

Here is why this is powerful. Imagine a shop page that shows twenty products. You write one `ProductCard` component, and use it twenty times with different data. If you later want to change how a card looks, you change it in one place, and all twenty cards change.
In React a component is just a JavaScript function that returns what should be shown. Here is the smallest example:
The strange part that looks like HTML inside JavaScript is called **JSX**. You will learn it in lesson 3. For now, just see that a component is a function, and its name starts with a capital letter.
Big idea 2: data flows down

Components get information from their parent through **props**. Props are like the settings you give to a function. A parent component can say to a `ProductCard`: “show this name and this price”. The card shows it. The card cannot change the props it receives. Data goes in one direction, from parent to child, which makes the app easy to follow. When something goes wrong, you can trace where the data came from.
Big idea 3: state

Some data changes while the person uses the page: the text in a search box, the items in a cart, or whether a menu is open. In React this changing data is called **state**. State belongs to a component. When the state changes, React draws the component again with the new data. This is called a **re-render**.

You do not tell the page “change this text to 5”. You change the state to 5, and the page shows 5 because the component describes the page from its state. This is the main idea of React, and the most common way to get stuck at first. If you remember one thing, remember this: **the screen is a result of the data**.
What is the virtual DOM?

The browser keeps the page as a tree of objects called the **DOM** (Document Object Model). Changing the real DOM can be slow if you do it too much. React keeps a light copy of the page in memory, called the **virtual DOM**. When your state changes, React makes a new virtual copy, compares it with the old one, and finds the small differences. Then it changes only those differences in the real page. This comparing step is called **reconciliation**.
You do not need to manage this. It is helpful to know it exists, because it explains why React is fast enough for large pages, and why you should never change the page by hand when React owns it.
React is a library, not a full framework

React only handles the screen. It does not decide how you send data to a server, how you move between pages, or how you style your app. For those jobs you choose other tools, such as React Router for pages. This gives you freedom, but it also means you must learn a few extra tools. This course covers the most important ones.

You may also hear about **Next.js**. It is a framework built on top of React that adds pages, server rendering and more. Learning React first is the right order, because Next.js is React with extra features.
Where is React used?

items: **Websites** such as online shops, news sites and dashboards.
**Mobile apps**, using a sister tool called React Native, which uses the same ideas.
**Admin tools and dashboards**, where data changes often and screens are full of forms and tables.
**Job markets:** React is one of the most requested skills in front end job adverts. Check adverts in your own country to see how common it is near you.

content.text: What you need to know before you start

You should know basic HTML and CSS, and the basics of JavaScript: variables, functions, arrays, objects and the `if` statement. If you know a little about arrow functions and array methods like `map`, that helps a lot, and we will explain them again when they come up. You do not need to be an expert. Many people learn JavaScript and React together.

If some JavaScript words are new, do not worry. Each lesson explains its own small steps, and each lesson has a short task to try. Practice is the best teacher, so type the code yourself instead of only reading it.
How this course is organised

items: **Start Here (lessons 1 to 10):** the basics: setup, JSX, components, props, state, events, lists, forms and styling.
**Hooks and Data (lessons 11 to 20):** useEffect, fetching data, refs, reducers, context, custom hooks, routing and forms.

**Advanced React (lessons 21 to 30):** speed, code splitting, error handling, state libraries, data libraries, testing, accessibility, new React 19 features, TypeScript and a final guide to real projects.

content.text: Each lesson uses short sentences and plain words, has code you can copy, a task and a small check list, and ends with a summary and common questions. Every lesson also has an animation at the top that shows the main idea step by step.
Tips for learning faster

items: **Type the code.** Copying and pasting teaches your fingers nothing. Typing makes you notice details.
**Break things on purpose.** Remove a bracket and read the error. Errors are the best teachers and you will meet them often.
**Build small things.** A counter, a to-do list, a notes app. Small finished projects beat big unfinished ones.
**Read errors slowly.** React usually tells you the file and line. Read the first line first.
**Come back.** If a lesson feels hard, finish it, move on, and return later. Ideas settle with time.

content.text: Your task

items: Write in one sentence what a component is, in your own words.
Think of a website you use daily. List three parts of it that could be components.
Think of one piece of data on that site that changes while you use it. That is state.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can explain components, props and state to a friend without using code.
You know why React says “describe the screen, do not change it by hand”.

content.text: Summary

items: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from small reusable components.
Props send data down from parent to child. State is data that changes, and a change makes the component draw again.
React keeps a virtual copy of the page and updates only what changed in the real page.
React handles the screen only. You add other tools for pages, data and more.

faqs.q: Is React a framework or a library?
faqs.a: React is a library. It handles the user interface only. A framework such as Next.js is built on React and adds more, like page routing and server rendering.

faqs.q: Do I need to learn JavaScript before React?
faqs.a: Yes, the basics. You need variables, functions, arrays, objects and conditions. You can learn a few more things, such as array methods and arrow functions, while learning React.

faqs.q: What is the virtual DOM in simple words?
faqs.a: It is a light copy of the page that React keeps in memory. React compares the old and new copy and changes only the small parts of the real page that are different.

faqs.q: Is React free?
faqs.a: Yes. React is free and open source. The tools in this course are free too.

lessons.title: Set Up React with Vite: Your First Project Step by Step
lessons.description: Install the tools, create your first React project with Vite, and learn what each file does. Run it in your browser.

content.text: Before you write React, you need a place to write and run it. In this lesson you will install the tools, create a new project and look at what each file does. After this lesson you will have a working React app on your computer that updates the moment you save a file.
What you need

items: **Node.js** (version 20 or newer). It lets JavaScript run on your computer, and it comes with **npm**, a tool that downloads packages.
**A code editor.** VS Code is free and a very popular choice.
**A browser** such as Chrome, Edge or Firefox.
**A terminal.** On Windows you can use PowerShell or the terminal inside VS Code. On Mac and Linux use the Terminal app.

content.text: To check Node.js, open the terminal and type the commands below. Each should print a version number. If the command is not found, install Node.js from its official website and open a new terminal window.

node --version
npm --version
What is Vite?

Writing React needs a **build tool**. Browsers do not understand JSX, and your code is split across many files. A build tool turns your files into something the browser can run, and gives you a fast development server. **Vite** (say “veet”) is the tool most people use today. It starts in a second, and when you save a file the browser updates without a full reload. This is called hot reloading.
Older tutorials may tell you to use **Create React App**. It is no longer the best choice for new projects, so we use Vite.
Create the project
In the terminal, go to the folder where you keep your projects and run this command. It asks a few questions. Choose **React** as the framework and **JavaScript** as the language.

npm create vite@latest my-first-app
cd my-first-app
npm install
npm run dev

`npm create vite@latest my-first-app` makes a new folder with the starter files. `npm install` downloads the packages the project needs into a folder called `node_modules`. `npm run dev` starts the development server. The terminal shows an address such as `http://localhost:5173`. Open it in your browser and you will see the Vite and React starter page with a counter button.
Leave the dev server running while you work. To stop it, press Ctrl and C in the terminal. To start it again, run `npm run dev`.
A tour of the folders and files
Open the project in VS Code. You will see a few files and folders. This is what matters:

items: **`index.html`**: the one page of your app. It has an empty `<div id="root">` and a script tag that loads your code. React draws everything inside that div.
**`package.json`**: the list of packages and the scripts like `dev` and `build`.
**`src/main.jsx`**: the front door. It tells React to draw your `App` component inside the root div.
**`src/App.jsx`**: your first component. This is where you will start writing.
**`src/App.css` and `src/index.css`**: styles.
**`public/`**: files that are copied as they are, such as the site icon.
**`node_modules/`**: the downloaded packages. Never edit it and never put it in Git.

content.text: Here is `main.jsx`. It is short, and it is worth understanding line by line:

items: `import ... from` brings code from another file or package. We bring in React tools and our own `App`.
`createRoot` connects React to the real element with the id `root` in `index.html`.
`.render(...)` tells React what to show. We show `<App />`.
`StrictMode` is a helper that gives extra warnings while you develop. It does nothing in the final site. In development it runs some code twice on purpose, to help you find mistakes.

content.text: Make your first change
Open `src/App.jsx`, delete everything in it, and write this simple component instead:
Save the file. The browser changes at once, with no reload. Try changing the words, and watch the page follow. That quick feedback is why Vite is nice to learn with.
Notice `export default App`. It makes this function available to other files, and `main.jsx` imports it. Each component usually lives in its own file, and the file name matches the component name.
The scripts in package.json

items: **`npm run dev`** starts the development server with hot reloading.
**`npm run build`** makes the final, small, fast files in a folder called `dist`. You upload these when you publish your site.
**`npm run preview`** serves the `dist` folder locally, so you can test the real build.
**`npm run lint`** (if present) checks your code for common mistakes with ESLint.

content.text: Useful editor and browser tools

items: **React Developer Tools** is a free browser extension. It adds two tabs to the browser tools: Components and Profiler. You can click a component and see its props and state. It is very useful for finding why something is not showing.
**ESLint** warns you when you break a rule, for example when you forget a key in a list.
**Prettier** formats your code so it looks the same every time. Many people turn on “format on save” in VS Code.

content.text: Common problems and quick fixes

items: **“npm is not recognised”:** Node.js is not installed, or the terminal was open before you installed it. Close it and open a new one.
**Blank page:** open the browser console (press F12) and read the first red error. It usually names the file and line.
**“Failed to resolve import”:** the file path or the file name has a typo. Paths are case-sensitive on many systems, so `app.jsx` and `App.jsx` can be different files.
**Port already in use:** Vite will choose the next free port, such as 5174, and show it in the terminal.
**Changes not showing:** check that you saved the file, and that the file you edit is the one `main.jsx` imports.

content.text: What happens when you run npm run dev?

It helps to know what is going on behind the scenes, so the tool does not feel like magic. When you run the command, Vite starts a small web server on your computer. When your browser asks for `index.html`, Vite sends it. The page then asks for `main.jsx`. Vite turns your JSX into plain JavaScript on the fly, and sends that to the browser. It does the same for every file the browser asks for. Because it only works on the files that are needed, it starts in a moment even for big projects.

When you save a file, Vite tells the browser which module changed, and the browser swaps just that piece. This is called **hot module replacement**. If you keep a counter at 7 and change the colour of a heading, the counter often stays at 7. That saves a lot of time every day.
Your task

items: Create a new Vite React project and run it in the browser.
Replace the content of `App.jsx` with your own heading and a short paragraph about yourself.
Create a new file `src/Footer.jsx` that exports a `Footer` component, then import and use it inside `App`.
Run `npm run build` and look inside the `dist` folder.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The browser shows your own heading without a reload when you save.
The footer text appears under your paragraph.
`npm run build` ends without errors and makes a `dist` folder.

content.text: Summary

items: Install Node.js, create a project with `npm create vite@latest`, run `npm install`, then `npm run dev`.
`index.html` has the root div, `main.jsx` connects React to it, and `App.jsx` is your first component.
Use `npm run build` to make the files you publish.
Install React Developer Tools. It helps you see props and state.

faqs.q: Why Vite and not Create React App?
faqs.a: Vite starts much faster, updates the page quicker when you save, and is actively used for new projects. Create React App is old and is no longer the recommended way to start.

faqs.q: What is node_modules and can I delete it?
faqs.a: It holds the packages your project uses. You can delete it safely and run npm install to get it back. Never put it in Git.

faqs.q: What is the difference between npm run dev and npm run build?
faqs.a: dev starts a fast local server for working on your app. build makes small optimised files in the dist folder that you upload to a host.

faqs.q: Do I have to use VS Code?
faqs.a: No. Any editor works. VS Code is free and has many helpful extensions, so most beginners choose it.

lessons.title: JSX Explained Simply: Write HTML Inside JavaScript
lessons.description: Learn JSX in simple steps: the rules, curly braces, className and styles, and the small mistakes every beginner makes.

content.text: JSX looks like HTML, but it lives inside a JavaScript file. It is the way most React developers describe what a component should show. At first it feels strange to mix HTML and JavaScript. After a short time it feels natural, because the code that decides what to show and the code that shows it sit together.
What JSX really is
JSX stands for JavaScript XML. It is not HTML, and browsers cannot read it. Your build tool (Vite) changes it into plain JavaScript before the browser sees it. This line of JSX:

const title =

Hello

;

becomes a normal function call, roughly `React.createElement('h1', { className: 'big' }, 'Hello')`. You never need to write that by hand. JSX is just a friendly way to write it. Knowing this explains the rules below, because JSX follows JavaScript rules, not HTML rules.
Rule 1: return one parent element
A component can return only one thing. If you want to return two headings, wrap them in a parent. The parent can be a `div`, or a **fragment**, which is an empty tag that adds nothing to the page.
The `<>` and `</>` are the fragment. Use a fragment when you do not want an extra `div` in your page. The round brackets after `return` let you write the JSX over many lines safely.
Rule 2: close every tag

In HTML you can write `
` or `` with no closing. In JSX every tag must be closed. Either write a closing tag, or end the tag with a slash:
Rule 3: use curly braces to show JavaScript

This is the most important JSX skill. Inside curly braces `{}` you can write any JavaScript **expression**, which is anything that gives a value. A variable, a calculation, a function call or a condition all work.

You can use curly braces in two places: **as the content** between tags (like `{name}` above), and **as the value of an attribute**, like `src={imageUrl}`. You cannot use them for the tag name, and you cannot put a statement such as `if` or `for` inside them. Statements do not give a value. Use a `?:` expression instead. You will see this in the lesson on conditional rendering.

Quotes give a fixed text: `alt="Logo"`. Curly braces give a changing value: `alt={product.name}`. A common mistake is writing `alt="{product.name}"`, which shows the words `{product.name}` instead of the name.
Rule 4: some attribute names are different
Because JSX is JavaScript, some HTML words are already taken by JavaScript. And all attribute names use camelCase, which means the first word is small and each next word starts with a capital letter.

items: `class` becomes **`className`**, because `class` is a JavaScript word.
`for` on a label becomes **`htmlFor`**.
`onclick` becomes **`onClick`**, and `onchange` becomes **`onChange`**.
`tabindex` becomes **`tabIndex`**, and `maxlength` becomes **`maxLength`**.

content.text: Good news: if you forget, React shows a clear warning in the browser console that names the right word.
Styles as objects

The `style` attribute does not take a string in React. It takes an object, and the object has its own curly braces. That is why you see double braces: the outer pair means “JavaScript here”, and the inner pair is the object.
Styled text
CSS names with a dash become camelCase (`font-size` becomes `fontSize`). Numbers are treated as pixels. For more than a few styles, use a CSS file instead, as lesson 10 shows.
Comments in JSX
Inside the tags you cannot use `//` or `<!-- -->`. Use curly braces and a normal comment:

{/* This comment will not show on the page */}

Visible text
Showing lists and objects

You can show strings and numbers directly. You can also show an array of strings, and React puts them next to each other. But you cannot show a plain object. If you try `{user}` where `user` is `{ name: 'Asha' }`, React throws an error that says objects are not valid as a React child. Show the parts you want instead: `{user.name}`.

Values like `true`, `false`, `null` and `undefined` show **nothing**. This is useful for conditions, and it is also a trap: the number `0` does show. We will see this trap again in the conditional rendering lesson.
Components in JSX

Tags that start with a small letter, like `div` or `p`, are normal HTML elements. Tags that start with a **capital letter**, like `Welcome` or `ProductCard`, are your own components. That is why component names must start with a capital: it is how React tells them apart.
Common beginner mistakes

items:
**Two parents:** returning `

` and `

` side by side without a wrapper. Fix: wrap them in a fragment.
**Forgetting to close a tag:** `<input>` must be `<input />`.
**Using `class`:** use `className`.
**Quotes around braces:** `src="{url}"` shows the text `{url}`. Remove the quotes.
**Lowercase component:** `<welcome />` is treated as an HTML tag. Use `<Welcome />`.
**Statements inside braces:** you cannot write `{if (x) ...}`. Use `{x ? a : b}`.

content.text: Walk through one component line by line
Let us read a small component slowly, as the browser and React would. Here it is again, with a bit more detail:

items: React calls the function `Profile()`. It is just a normal function call.
The first two lines make two ordinary variables. There is nothing special about them yet.
The `return` gives back JSX. Vite has already changed it into function calls, so the result is a plain description of a `section` with an `h2` and a `p`.
When React meets `{name}`, it runs the JavaScript inside the braces, gets the text `Asha`, and puts it in the heading.
For `{skills.length}`, it works out the number 2 and shows it inside the sentence.
React then updates the real page so it matches this description.

content.text: Once you see JSX as “JavaScript that describes the page”, the rules stop feeling random. A tag name that starts with a capital letter is a function to call. Curly braces are a hole where JavaScript goes. And one parent is needed because a function can return only one value.
Your task

items: Make a component `Card` with a name, a job title and a year of birth stored in variables. Show them, and show the age using a calculation.
Add an image with `alt` text taken from the name variable.
Give one heading an inline style with a colour and a bigger font size.
Break a rule on purpose (remove a closing tag) and read the error message.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The card shows the name, the job title and a correct age.
Your image has alt text that changes if you change the variable.
You can say in your own words why `class` is `className`.

content.text: Summary

items: JSX is a way to write HTML-like code inside JavaScript. Vite turns it into plain JavaScript.
Return one parent (or a fragment), close all tags, and use camelCase attributes such as `className` and `onClick`.
Use `{}` to show any JavaScript expression. The style attribute takes an object.
Component names start with a capital letter.

faqs.q: Is JSX required to use React?
faqs.a: No, but almost everyone uses it. It is much easier to read than the plain JavaScript it becomes.

faqs.q: Why do I see double curly braces in style?
faqs.a: The outer braces mean JavaScript starts here. The inner braces are the JavaScript object that holds the styles.

faqs.q: Why does my component not show up?
faqs.a: Check that its name starts with a capital letter, that you imported it, and that you wrote it as a tag, like <Welcome />, not as Welcome.

faqs.q: What is a fragment?
faqs.a: A fragment, written <>...</>, groups elements without adding an extra element to the page.

lessons.title: React Components and Props Explained with Examples
lessons.description: Build components and send data to them with props. Learn defaults, children, and how to split a page into small parts.

content.text: Components are the heart of React. Once you can split a page into components and pass data between them, you can build almost any screen. This lesson shows how, with small, clear examples.
What is a component?

A component is a JavaScript function that returns JSX. It has a name that starts with a capital letter. You use it like an HTML tag. Components can be used again and again, and they can use other components inside them.
This shows the greeting three times. But three identical greetings are not very useful. We want each greeting to show a different name. That is the job of props.
Props: giving data to a component
**Props** (short for properties) are the inputs of a component, like the arguments of a function. The parent writes them like HTML attributes. The child receives them as one object.

Notice the difference between `name="Asha"` (text, in quotes) and `age={24}` (a number, in curly braces). If the value is not a plain string, use curly braces. This is true for numbers, booleans, arrays, objects and functions.
Destructuring props
Writing `props.name` again and again is long. Most people use **destructuring**, a JavaScript feature that pulls values out of an object into variables. You do it right in the function brackets:
This does exactly the same, and it also shows at the top which props the component needs. We will use this style from now on.
Default values
If a parent forgets to pass a prop, its value is `undefined`. You can give a default value in the destructuring:
Props are read-only

A component must never change its own props. Props belong to the parent. If a child needs data that changes, it uses **state**, which you will meet in the next lesson. This rule keeps data flow simple: data goes down, and you can always find where a value came from. If you try to assign `props.name = 'x'`, React will give an error.
Passing different kinds of values

<Profile
  name="Asha"
  isAdmin={true}
  skills={['React', 'CSS', 'SQL']}
  address={{ city: 'Pune', country: 'India' }}
  onSave={() => console.log('saved')}
/>

A prop can be text, a number, a true or false value, an array, an object, or even a function. Passing a function is how a child tells its parent that something happened, as you will see in the lessons on events and lifting state.
For a `true` prop you can write just the name: `<Profile isAdmin />` means the same as `isAdmin={true}`.
Children: putting content inside a component
Sometimes you want to put things between the opening and closing tags of your component, like you do with a `div`. React gives these to the component as a special prop called `children`.
The `Card` does not know what is inside it. This makes it a very flexible building block. Boxes, layouts, modals and panels are often made this way.
Splitting a page into components
A good habit: look at a design and draw boxes around the parts that repeat, or that have one clear job. Each box can be a component. Here is a small profile page split into pieces:

A rule of thumb: if a part of the screen is used in more than one place, or if a function grows over about fifty lines, think about splitting it. Do not split too early either. A tiny component used once is not always better.
Where to put components

items: Put each component in its own file, named after it: `Avatar.jsx` holds `Avatar`.
Use `export default Avatar;` at the bottom, and `import Avatar from './Avatar.jsx';` at the top of the file that uses it.
Group files in folders such as `src/components`. Keep it simple until the project grows.

content.text: **Never define a component inside another component.** It looks like it works, but React will make a new copy on every draw, and any state inside it is lost. Always write components at the top level of a file.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting the capital letter, so `<card>` is treated as an HTML tag.
Writing `age="24"` and then trying to add to it: it is text, not a number. Use `age={24}`.
Changing props inside the child. Copy the value into state if you need to change it.
Defining a component inside another one.
Passing a function call instead of a function: `onSave={save()}` runs it at once. Use `onSave={save}` or `onSave={() => save(id)}`.

content.text: A complete example, step by step
Let us build a small team page, and watch how props travel. We have three pieces: an `App` that owns the data, a `TeamList` that shows many people, and a `Person` that shows one.

Follow the data. `App` makes the list and passes it to `TeamList` as the prop `people`. `TeamList` goes through the list and, for each item, passes `name` and `role` to a `Person`. `Person` finally shows them. The data moves **down**, one level at a time, and nobody changes it on the way. If a name looks wrong on the page, you know to look at the data in `App`.

Notice how each piece is easy to understand alone. `Person` knows nothing about teams. You could use it on an about page, in a contact list or in a chat. This is the real power of components: small, simple and used in many places.
Questions beginners often ask
**Can a component return nothing?** Yes. Return `null` and it shows nothing. This is useful for a component that decides not to appear, such as a banner with no message.

**How do I know when to make a new component?** Make one when a piece of the screen repeats, when it has one clear job, or when a component becomes hard to read. If you can give a part a good short name, such as `Avatar` or `PriceTag`, it is a good candidate.
**Why is my component name in capital letters?** It is how React tells your own components from HTML tags. `<card />` is looked up as an HTML tag called card, but `<Card />` is your function.
**Can props have the same name as HTML attributes?** Yes. Props are your own names. Many people use `title`, `src` and `label`. Just remember that a prop does nothing until your component uses it.
Your task

items: Create a `ProductCard` component that takes `name`, `price` and an optional `inStock` prop (default `true`). Show “Out of stock” when it is false.
Use it three times with different data.
Create a `Box` component that wraps its `children` in a border, and put a `ProductCard` inside it.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Three different cards appear on the page.
Changing `inStock` to `false` changes the message.
The `Box` draws a border around any content you put inside.

content.text: Summary

items: A component is a function with a capital letter that returns JSX.
Props are read-only inputs. Use destructuring, defaults and curly braces for non-text values.
`children` is the content placed inside a component's tags.
Split the screen into small pieces, each in its own file, and never define a component inside another.

faqs.q: What is the difference between props and state?
faqs.a: Props come from the parent and cannot be changed by the child. State belongs to the component and can change over time.

faqs.q: Can I pass a function as a prop?
faqs.a: Yes. It is how a child component tells its parent that something happened, such as a button click.

faqs.q: How many props are too many?
faqs.a: There is no fixed number, but if a component needs many props, think about passing one object, or splitting it into smaller components.

faqs.q: Why can I not change props?
faqs.a: Props belong to the parent. Letting children change them would make data hard to follow. Use state for data that changes.

lessons.title: React useState Explained: Make Your Page React to Change
lessons.description: Learn state with useState using a counter, a toggle and a text box, and why you must never change state directly.

content.text: So far our components show fixed data. Real pages change: a counter goes up, a menu opens, a message appears. To remember data that changes, a component needs **state**. In this lesson you will learn state with the `useState` hook, step by step, using small examples.
Why a normal variable does not work
Let us try to build a counter with a plain variable. It looks right, but it does not work:

If you click, the console shows 1, 2, 3, but the button always says 0. There are two reasons. First, React does not know that `count` changed, so it does not draw the component again. Second, even if it did, a function component starts from the top each time it is drawn, so `let count = 0` would run again and reset the number. We need a place where React can keep the value safe between draws, and where changing it tells React to draw again. That place is state.
The useState hook
A **hook** is a special function whose name starts with `use`. Hooks let a component use React features. `useState` gives a component a piece of state.
Let us read the key line, `const [count, setCount] = useState(0);`:

items: `useState(0)` creates a piece of state and says its **first value is 0**.
It returns an array with two things. The first is the **current value**, which we call `count`. The second is a **function to change it**, which we call `setCount`.
We use array destructuring to give them names. You can choose any names, but the pattern `[thing, setThing]` is the usual way.

content.text: When you click, `setCount(count + 1)` tells React: “the new value is one more”. React stores it, draws the component again, and this time `count` is 1. The button shows “Clicked 1 times”. The same happens for each click.
What happens when state changes

items: You call the setter function, for example `setCount(5)`.
React saves the new value.
React calls your component function again (a re-render).
This time `useState` gives back the new value.
React compares the new result with the old one and updates the page where it is different.

content.text: The big idea: you never change the page yourself. You change the state, and the page follows.
State can be any type
State is not only for numbers. Here are a few common kinds:

const [name, setName] = useState('');            // text
const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false);     // true or false
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);          // a list
const [user, setUser] = useState(null);          // an object, or nothing yet
const [form, setForm] = useState({ email: '', age: 0 });  // an object
Example: a toggle

Each click flips `isOpen` between `true` and `false`. The text on the button and the list both depend on it. You wrote no code to show or hide anything by hand. You only described what to show for each value.
Example: a text box

Every key press makes a change event. The handler reads the new text with `event.target.value` and puts it in state. The input shows what is in state through its `value`. This pattern is called a **controlled input**, and the forms lesson explains it fully.
The golden rule: never change state directly

State is read-only. You must always use the setter. If you write `count = count + 1` or `items.push('x')`, React does not notice, and the screen does not change. For numbers and text this is easy. For arrays and objects, you must **make a new copy** and pass the copy to the setter.

The three dots `...` are called the **spread** syntax. They copy all the items of an array, or all the fields of an object, into a new one. React decides whether something changed by checking if the value is a **new** object, so a copy is required. This idea is called **immutability**, and it is one of the most important habits to learn.
State updates are not instant
Calling the setter does not change the variable in the code that is running right now. It asks React to draw again with the new value. This surprises many beginners:
The console shows the old number, because that variable belongs to the draw that is already finished. The new value arrives in the next draw.

There is a second problem. If you call `setCount(count + 1)` three times in a row, you get +1, not +3, because each call used the same old `count`. When the new value depends on the old value, pass a function. React gives it the latest value:
Rule of thumb: if the new state depends on the old state, use the function form `setX((old) => ...)`.
Where should state live?

items: Each `useState` call belongs to one component. Two copies of `Counter` have two separate counts.
Keep state as **small** as you can. Do not store data you can work out from other data. For example, store the list, and calculate its length when you need it.
If two components need the same state, move it to their closest shared parent. Lesson 14 covers this.

content.text: Also remember the rules of hooks: call them only at the **top level** of a component, never inside an `if`, a loop, or a nested function. And call them only inside components or custom hooks. React depends on the order of the hook calls staying the same on every draw.
Common mistakes

items: Changing state directly (`count++`, `items.push(...)`).
Forgetting to copy an object or array before changing it.
Expecting the variable to change right after calling the setter.
Calling hooks inside conditions or loops.
Storing something you could calculate, which makes two values that can get out of step.

content.text: One more example: a like button
To finish, here is a small component that joins three ideas from this lesson: state, an event and a conditional message.

There are two pieces of state, and both change in one click. React waits until the handler finishes, and then draws once. The text on the button comes from state, and `aria-pressed` tells screen readers whether the button is on or off. Try to find the other places in your own projects where a small piece of state like this would help.
Your task

items: Build a counter with three buttons: add one, subtract one, and reset to zero.
Build a to-do list with an input and an Add button. Keep the list in state and add items using the spread syntax.
Add a Remove button to each item using `filter`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The counter never goes wrong when you click quickly.
New to-do items appear at once and the input still works.
Removing an item removes only that item.

content.text: Summary

items: State is data that changes. `useState(initial)` returns the value and a setter.
A call to the setter makes React draw the component again with the new value.
Never change state directly. Make a new array or object with spread, `map` or `filter`.
If the new value depends on the old one, use `setX((old) => ...)`.

faqs.q: Why do I need useState instead of a normal variable?
faqs.a: A normal variable resets every time the component is drawn, and changing it does not tell React to draw again. State is kept safe between draws, and changing it with the setter makes React update the screen.

faqs.q: Why is my state not updating right after I set it?
faqs.a: The setter asks React to draw again with the new value. The variable in the running code still holds the old value. The new one is available in the next draw.

faqs.q: Can I have many useState calls in one component?
faqs.a: Yes. Use one for each separate piece of data, or use one object when the pieces always change together.

faqs.q: What is the difference between useState and a variable inside useEffect?
faqs.a: State is meant for data that the screen shows. A normal variable or a ref is better for values that do not need to cause a redraw.

lessons.title: Handling Events in React: Clicks, Typing and Forms Made Simple
lessons.description: React to clicks, typing and form submit. Learn the event object, how to pass values, and the most common event mistakes.

content.text: A page that never reacts is just a poster. Events are how people talk to your app: they click, type, hover, press keys and submit forms. In React, handling events is simple and looks like HTML, with a few small differences. This lesson shows each of them.
Your first event handler
To react to a click, give the element an `onClick` prop. Its value is the **function** to run when the click happens.
A good habit is to start the name of the handler with `handle`, such as `handleClick` or `handleSubmit`. It makes your code easy to read.
The most common mistake: calling the function
Look at the difference between these two lines:

<button onClick={handleClick}>Right</button>      {/* passes the function */}
<button onClick={handleClick()}>Wrong</button>    {/* runs it at once */}

The wrong version runs `handleClick()` while the page is being drawn, and passes its result to the button. Remember: **pass the function, do not call it.** Without brackets you give React the function to call later. With brackets you call it now.
Inline handlers
For very short actions, you can write the function directly. An arrow function is the usual way:
<button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Add</button>
If your handler is longer than one line, write a named function above, so the JSX stays easy to read.
Passing an argument
Often you need to tell the handler which item was clicked. Wrap the call in an arrow function:
The arrow function `() => onRemove(item.id)` waits until the click, then calls `onRemove` with the right id. Each button gets its own arrow function, so each remembers its own item.
The event object
React gives your handler one argument: the **event object**. It holds details about what happened. The most useful parts are:

items: `event.target`: the element that caused the event. For an input, `event.target.value` is the text in it.
`event.preventDefault()`: stops the browser's normal action, such as reloading the page when a form is submitted.
`event.key`: for key events, the key that was pressed, such as `'Enter'`.
`event.stopPropagation()`: stops the event from reaching parent elements.

content.text: Form submit
A form that is submitted makes the browser reload the page, which would throw away your state. Stop that with `preventDefault`:
Use `onSubmit` on the `form`, not `onClick` on the button. That way the form also works when the person presses Enter, and it works with screen readers and keyboards.
Common events

items: `onClick`: a click or tap.
`onChange`: the value of an input changed. In React it fires on every key press.
`onSubmit`: a form was submitted.
`onKeyDown` and `onKeyUp`: a key was pressed or released.
`onMouseEnter` and `onMouseLeave`: the pointer moved onto or off an element.
`onFocus` and `onBlur`: an element got or lost focus.

content.text: Events travel up (bubbling)

When you click a button inside a box, the click first happens on the button, then **bubbles up** to the box and then to its parents. If both have an `onClick`, both run. If you do not want the parent to know, call `event.stopPropagation()` in the child.
console.log('box clicked')}>
Child tells parent: functions as props

A child component cannot change the state of its parent directly. Instead the parent passes a **function** as a prop, and the child calls it when something happens. This is how data flows up in React.
A common name for such props is `onSomething`, like `onLike`, `onSave` or `onDelete`. It tells the reader that this prop is an event that the parent can listen to.
Good habits for events

items: Use real `button` elements for clicks, not a `div`. Buttons work with the keyboard and with screen readers for free. Add `type="button"` to buttons inside forms that should not submit.
Keep handlers short. If a handler grows, move the work into a normal function.
Do not forget `preventDefault` in form submit handlers.
Disable a button while a request is running, so people cannot click twice.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Writing `onclick` (small letters). It must be `onClick`.
Calling the function: `onClick={save()}`.
Forgetting `event.preventDefault()` in a form, and then wondering why the page reloads.
Using a `div` with `onClick` for something that is really a button.
Reading `event` inside a delayed function after it ended. Copy what you need first: `const value = event.target.value`.

content.text: A worked example: a tiny color picker
Let us put several events in one small component. It has buttons that choose a colour, a text box for a label, and a form that saves the choice.

There are four kinds of events in this one small component: `onClick` on the colour buttons (with an argument), `onChange` on the input, `onSubmit` on the form, and the state updates that follow. Each event calls a function, the function changes state, and React draws the new screen. That loop is how every React app works. Notice also that the colour buttons have `type="button"`, so they do not submit the form by mistake.
Questions beginners often ask

**Why do I use an arrow function in onClick sometimes and not other times?** If the handler needs no argument, pass the function name: `onClick={handleSave}`. If you need to give it an argument, such as an id, wrap the call: `onClick={() => handleRemove(id)}`. The wrapper waits until the click before it calls your function.

**What is the difference between onChange and onInput?** In React you almost always use `onChange`. It fires on every key press in a text input, which is what you want for keeping state in step with the field.

**Can I use the same handler for many buttons?** Yes. Pass different arguments in the arrow function, or read information from the event, such as `event.currentTarget.dataset.id`. One handler for many items keeps your code short.

**Why does my page reload when I press a button in a form?** A button inside a form submits it by default. Add `type="button"` to buttons that should not submit, and use `event.preventDefault()` in the submit handler.
Your task

items: Make a button that toggles a message between “On” and “Off”.
Make a text box that shows how many characters have been typed.
Make a small form with a name field. On submit, add the name to a list on the page, and clear the input.
Add a child component `DeleteButton` that calls an `onDelete` prop, and use it to remove names.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The page does not reload when you submit the form.
Pressing Enter in the input submits the form.
Deleting a name removes only that name.

content.text: Summary

items: Events use camelCase props such as `onClick`. Pass a function, do not call it.
Use an arrow function to pass arguments: `() => remove(id)`.
The event object gives `target.value`, `key` and `preventDefault()`.
Child components tell the parent about events through function props.

faqs.q: Why does my onClick run when the page loads?
faqs.a: You wrote onClick={handleClick()}, which calls the function at once. Write onClick={handleClick} or onClick={() => handleClick()}.

faqs.q: What is event.preventDefault() for?
faqs.a: It stops the normal browser action. In a form it stops the page from reloading when the form is submitted.

faqs.q: What is the difference between onChange in React and in HTML?
faqs.a: In React, onChange fires on every key press in a text input, so you can keep state in step with what the person types.

faqs.q: How does a child component change the parent state?
faqs.a: The parent passes a function as a prop. The child calls it, and the parent changes its own state inside that function.

lessons.title: Conditional Rendering in React: Show and Hide Things the Easy Way
lessons.description: Show different content with if, ternary, && and early return. Build loading, empty and error screens the easy way.

content.text: Real pages show different things at different times. A person who is signed in sees their name, and a visitor sees a Sign in button. A list that is empty shows a friendly message. A page that is loading shows a spinner. Showing different content depending on a condition is called **conditional rendering**. In React there is no special syntax for it. You use plain JavaScript, which makes it easy to learn.
Way 1: an if statement before the return
A component is a function, so you can use `if` before you return. This is the clearest way when the screens are very different.
When the first `return` runs, the function stops, so the second line is only reached when `isLoggedIn` is false. This idea is called an **early return**, and it keeps code flat and easy to read.
Way 2: the ternary operator
Inside JSX you cannot write an `if` statement, because curly braces accept only expressions. The **ternary operator** is an expression with three parts: `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`.

You can use a ternary for text, for attribute values, and for whole pieces of JSX. If you find yourself nesting one ternary inside another, stop: it becomes very hard to read. Use `if` or a small component instead.
Way 3: the && operator

When you want to show something **or nothing**, use `&&`. In JavaScript, `a && b` gives `b` if `a` is true, and gives `a` if it is false. React shows nothing for `false`, so this works as a simple “show this only if” rule.

Watch out for the number zero. If `unread` is 0, then `unread && ...` gives `0`, and React **shows the number 0** on the page. That is why we wrote `unread > 0 &&`, which gives a real true or false. Always make the left side a true or false value.
Way 4: save JSX in a variable
For bigger choices, you can pick the content first and then show it:
Another handy way is an object that maps a value to a component:
The three screens every data page needs

When a page loads data, it is always in one of three situations: it is still loading, it failed, or it has data. If you forget one of them, people see a blank page or a crash. A good pattern is to handle the unusual cases first with early returns:

Because each unusual case returns early, the last part of the function only has to think about the happy case. This is much easier to read than a deep chain of `if` and `else`. Also notice the **empty state**: an empty list is not an error, and a helpful message with a next step is kinder than a blank space.
Showing nothing
A component can return `null` to show nothing. This is useful when a component decides not to appear:
Hiding with CSS or removing from the page?

With conditional rendering, a hidden element is **removed** from the page, and any state inside it is lost. When it comes back, it starts fresh. If you want to keep the state, or want a fade animation, you can hide the element with CSS instead (for example the `hidden` attribute or `display: none`). Choose based on what you need:

items: **Remove it** (conditional rendering): saves work and memory, resets the state.
**Hide it** (CSS): keeps the state, allows animation, but the component still exists.

content.text: Choosing between the ways

items: Two very different screens: **early return** with `if`.
Choose between two small things inside JSX: **ternary**.
Show something or nothing: **&&** with a true/false left side.
Many choices: a variable with `if/else`, a `switch`, or an object map.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: `{count && <List />}` when `count` can be `0`. It shows `0`. Use `count > 0 &&`.
Nested ternaries that nobody can read. Use `if` or split into components.
Trying to write `{if (x) {...}}` in JSX. Statements are not allowed inside braces.
Forgetting the empty and error cases for data pages.
Reading `user.name` when `user` can be `null`. Check `user &&` first, or use `user?.name`.

content.text: The last item uses **optional chaining**, written `?.`. It stops safely and gives `undefined` if the value before it is `null` or `undefined`, instead of crashing. It is very useful when data has not arrived yet.
Putting it together: a small account menu
Here is a menu that uses several of the ideas from this lesson at once: an early return, a ternary and `&&`.

Each line has one clear job. The first two lines handle the unusual cases and finish early. After that, the code only thinks about a signed-in user. This habit, handling the odd cases first, keeps components flat and easy to read, even when they grow.
Questions beginners often ask

**Which way should I choose?** Pick the one that makes the code easiest to read. A short ternary for text, `&&` for show-or-nothing, and early returns for whole screens. If you cannot read your own condition in one go, split it into a variable with a clear name, such as `const canEdit = user && user.isAdmin;`.
**Does hidden content still cost anything?** Content that is not rendered costs nothing, because it is not in the page. Content hidden with CSS is still in the page, and its component still runs.

**Can I render different components in a loop?** Yes. Inside `map`, you can use a ternary or an object map to choose a component for each item, for example a `Photo` or a `Video` depending on the `type` field.
**Is it fine to use switch?** Yes. A `switch` before the `return` is good for many cases. Keep each case short, and move big pieces into their own components.
Your task

items: Make a `LoginButton` that shows “Log in” when signed out and “Log out” when signed in, using a ternary and state.
Make a `Notice` component that returns `null` when its `message` prop is empty.
Make a `UserList` that shows Loading, an error message, an empty message, or the list, depending on three props.
Test the zero trap: show a count with `count && ...` and then fix it.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Each situation shows the right screen when you change the props by hand.
No stray `0` appears on the page.
No error in the console when the data is empty.

content.text: Summary

items: Conditional rendering is plain JavaScript: `if`, ternary `?:` and `&&`.
Use early returns for loading, error and empty screens.
Make the left side of `&&` a real true or false to avoid the stray `0`.
Return `null` to show nothing, and use `?.` to read values that may be missing.

faqs.q: Can I use if inside JSX?
faqs.a: No, JSX curly braces accept expressions only. Use a ternary (condition ? a : b) or && inside JSX, or use if before the return.

faqs.q: Why does my page show a 0?
faqs.a: You wrote something like {count && <X />} and count was 0. React shows the number 0. Write {count > 0 && <X />}.

faqs.q: Does a hidden component keep its state?
faqs.a: If you remove it with conditional rendering, no, the state is lost. If you only hide it with CSS, the component stays and keeps its state.

faqs.q: What does ?. mean?
faqs.a: It is optional chaining. user?.name gives undefined if user is null or undefined, instead of crashing.

First check loading. If it is loading, return early with a loading message.
Next check for an error. If there is one, show a clear message and a way to retry.

lessons.title: Rendering Lists in React: map(), Keys, Filter and Sort Explained
lessons.description: Show lists with map, learn why keys matter, and filter, sort, add and remove items without breaking your state.

content.text: Almost every real app shows lists: products, messages, tasks, comments, search results. In React, you turn an array of data into a list of elements. You do it with a JavaScript method you may already know: `map`. This lesson explains how, and also the one thing beginners often miss: the **key**.
The map method in one minute
`map` goes through an array and makes a new array by running a function on each item. It does not change the original array.
In React we use `map` to turn data into JSX. React knows how to show an array of elements, one after the other.
Showing a list

The curly braces open JavaScript inside the `ul`. `fruits.map(...)` gives an array of `li` elements, and React shows them. Notice the round brackets after the arrow: they let us return JSX over several lines.
A list of objects
Most real lists are arrays of objects. Each object has an `id` that makes it unique:

Here every item becomes a `ProductCard` component. This is the most common shape: a list component that maps data into item components. Note that the `key` goes on the element returned **directly inside the map**, here the `ProductCard`.
What is a key and why does React want it?

If you forget the key, React shows a warning in the console: “Each child in a list should have a unique key”. A **key** is a special prop that gives each item a name. React uses it to remember which item is which, between draws.

Imagine a list of three tasks, and you delete the first one. Without keys, React only knows there are now two items in a row, and may reuse the wrong boxes. With keys, React knows that task 1 is gone, and tasks 2 and 3 are the same as before. This matters most when items have state, such as an input with typed text, or a checkbox. Without good keys, the typed text can jump to the wrong item.
A key is not passed as a prop. Inside the component you cannot read `props.key`. If you need the id, pass it again with another name, such as `id={product.id}`.
Rules for keys

items: Keys must be **unique among the siblings** in the same list. They do not need to be unique in the whole app.
Keys must be **stable**: the same item should keep the same key every time. Use an id from your data, such as a database id.
**Do not make keys with `Math.random()`.** A new key every draw makes React throw away and re-make every item, which is slow and loses state.
**Avoid the array index** as a key when the list can be re-ordered, filtered or changed. Index as a key is fine only for a list that never changes.

content.text: If your data has no ids, give each item an id when you **create** it, for example with `crypto.randomUUID()`, and keep it in the data.
Keys with fragments
If each item needs to return two elements side by side, you use a fragment. The short form `<>` cannot take a key, so use the long form:
Filtering a list

`filter` makes a new array with only the items that pass a test. Combine it with `map` to show only some items. Do not remove items from your data just to hide them. Keep the full list in state, and filter when you draw.
The list `visible` is not state. It is **calculated** from state and props during the draw. This is a good habit: do not store in state what you can calculate.
Sorting a list

Careful: the `sort` method **changes the array in place**. If you call it on state or props, you break the rule that data must not be changed. Make a copy first with the spread syntax, or use `toSorted` in modern browsers:

const sorted = [...products].sort((a, b) => a.price - b.price);
// or: const sorted = products.toSorted((a, b) => a.price - b.price);
For text, sort with `a.name.localeCompare(b.name)`, which also handles letters from other languages correctly.
Showing a message for an empty list
When the list is empty, show something helpful, as the conditional rendering lesson explained:
Adding and removing items
Because state must not be changed directly, adding and removing use a new array:
You will use these three lines in almost every project you build. It is worth typing them until they feel natural.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting the `key` and ignoring the warning.
Putting the key on the wrong element: it belongs on the outermost element returned by `map`.
Using the index as a key in a list that changes, which causes input values to jump around.
Calling `sort` or `reverse` on state without copying.
Writing `forEach` instead of `map`. `forEach` returns nothing, so nothing is shown.

content.text: Why the key matters: a small experiment

You can see the effect of keys yourself. Make a list of three items where each has an input box. Use the **index** as the key, and add a button that adds a new item at the **start** of the list. Type something in the first box, and then press the button. You will notice that the text you typed stays in the first position, even though it now belongs to a different item. React matched the boxes by position, so the typed text stayed in the first box.

Now change the key to the item's `id` and try again. The typed text moves along with its item, which is what you expect. This is the whole story of keys: they tell React which item is which, so the right state stays with the right item. It is a small change in the code and prevents very confusing bugs.
Your task

items: Make a list of five books with id, title and year. Show them with `map` and correct keys.
Add a text box that filters the books by title.
Add a button that sorts by year, without changing the original array.
Add a message for when no book matches.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The console has no key warning.
Typing in the filter updates the list at once.
The sort button does not change the order of the original data.

content.text: Summary

items: Use `array.map(item => <Element key={item.id} />)` to show lists.
Keys must be unique, stable and come from your data. Avoid random keys, and avoid the index for changing lists.
Filter and sort a **copy**. Keep the full list in state, and calculate what to show.
Add, remove and change items by making new arrays with spread, `filter` and `map`.

faqs.q: Why does React need keys?
faqs.a: Keys let React tell which item is which between draws, so it can update, move or remove the right items and keep their state correct.

faqs.q: Can I use the array index as the key?
faqs.a: Only for a list that never changes order, and never has items added or removed in the middle. Otherwise use a stable id from your data.

faqs.q: Why can I not read props.key?
faqs.a: Key is used by React itself and is not passed to your component. Pass the value again under another name if you need it.

faqs.q: How do I show nothing for an empty list?
faqs.a: Check the length. If it is zero, show a friendly message instead of an empty list.

map turns each object into an element, such as an li or a card.

lessons.title: React Forms and Controlled Inputs: Text, Checkbox, Select and Submit
lessons.description: Build forms the React way. Use controlled inputs, checkboxes, selects, simple checks and helpful error messages.

content.text: Forms are how people give data to your app: they sign up, search, write comments and pay. In plain HTML the browser keeps the text typed in each input. In React we usually keep it in **state** instead, so the screen and the data always agree. This lesson teaches the most common way, called **controlled inputs**.
Controlled input: the idea
A controlled input gets its value from React state, and tells React about every change. Two props make this work: `value` (what to show) and `onChange` (what to do when the person types).

Follow the loop: the person types a letter, `onChange` runs, `setName` saves the new text in state, React draws again, and the input shows the new `value`. The state is the **single source of truth**. If you set `value` but forget `onChange`, the input becomes read-only and React warns you.

Do you see the `label` with `htmlFor`? It connects the text to the input. Clicking the label focuses the input, and screen readers read the label out. Always add one. A placeholder is not a replacement for a label.
Many fields, one state object
A form with ten fields should not need ten `useState` calls and ten handlers. Use one object, and give each input a `name`. One handler can then update any field:

The strange `[name]: value` is a **computed property name**. It uses the value of the variable `name` (such as `'email'`) as the key. And `...form` copies all the old fields first, so only one field is replaced. Remember the rule: never change state directly.
Checkboxes
A checkbox uses `checked` instead of `value`, and you read `event.target.checked`:

const [agree, setAgree] = useState(false);

<label>
  <input type="checkbox" checked={agree} onChange={(e) => setAgree(e.target.checked)} />
  I accept the terms
</label>
<button disabled={!agree}>Continue</button>
The `disabled` prop is tied to state, so the button works only after the box is ticked. This is a small taste of how state controls the page.
Select (dropdown)
In React a select also uses `value` on the `select` element itself, not `selected` on each option:

<select value={country} onChange={(e) => setCountry(e.target.value)}>
  <option value="India">India</option>
  <option value="UK">United Kingdom</option>
  <option value="Canada">Canada</option>
</select>
Radio buttons
Radio buttons share one state value. Each radio is checked when its own value equals the state:
Textarea
In HTML, a textarea has its text between tags. In React it is like an input: use `value` and `onChange`, and write it as a self-closing tag or with `value`:
<textarea value={message} onChange={(e) => setMessage(e.target.value)} rows={4} />
Simple validation
Validation means checking that what the person typed makes sense. Check on submit, and show a clear message next to the field. Keep the errors in state:

items: `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` help screen readers know that the field has a problem and what it is.
`role="alert"` makes screen readers read the message when it appears.
Write messages that help: say what to do, not only what went wrong.
**Always validate again on the server.** The browser can be bypassed, so client checks are only a convenience.

content.text: Clearing the form after submit
Because the form lives in state, clearing it is easy: set the state back to the starting value. Keep that value in one constant so you can reuse it.
Controlled or uncontrolled?

There is another way: **uncontrolled** inputs, where the browser keeps the value and you read it only when needed, with a ref or with `FormData`. It is shorter for simple forms and for very large forms. Lesson 19 shows it. For most forms where you check the text as people type, controlled inputs are the easiest to understand.
Common mistakes

items: Setting `value` without `onChange`: the field becomes impossible to type in.
Starting with `undefined`: `useState()` with no value makes the input uncontrolled, then controlled, and React warns. Start with `''`.
Changing the form object directly instead of copying it.
Using `onClick` on the submit button instead of `onSubmit` on the form.
Forgetting the label, which hurts people who use screen readers.

content.text: Walk through a keystroke
Controlled inputs are easier to trust when you follow one key press from start to finish. Say the person types the letter “A” in an empty name field.

items: The browser fires a change event on the input.
React calls your `onChange` handler with the event. `event.target.value` is now `A`.
Your handler calls `setName('A')`. React stores the new value and plans a draw.
React calls your component again. This time `name` is `A`.
The input is drawn with `value={name}`, so it shows `A`. Everything that uses `name`, such as a counter of characters, shows the new value too.

content.text: This happens fast enough that you never notice it. The key idea is that the input never keeps its own text. It always shows what is in state. That is why the state and the screen cannot disagree, and why you can do things like change the text to capitals as people type, limit the length, or clear the field from code.
A small example: capital letters and a limit

<input
  value={code}
  onChange={(e) => setCode(e.target.value.toUpperCase().slice(0, 6))}
  placeholder="Enter a six letter code"
/>

The text is changed **before** it is saved in state, so the field always shows capital letters and never more than six of them. With a normal uncontrolled input you would need extra code to do this. Because the input is controlled, it is one line.
Questions beginners often ask
**Do I need a library for forms?** Not for small forms. Controlled inputs and a simple validation function are enough. Look at a library when your forms are large, have many steps or have many rules.

**Why does my number input give text?** The value of every input is text, even for `type="number"`. Convert it with `Number(value)` when you need a number, and think about what to do when the field is empty.

**How do I show a password?** Keep a true or false state, such as `show`, and set `type={show ? "text" : "password"}`. Add a button with a clear label like “Show password”, and tell screen readers its state with `aria-pressed`.

**How do I stop people from sending a form twice?** Keep a `sending` state. Set it to true at the start of submit, disable the button while it is true, and set it to false when the request ends, whether it worked or not.
Your task

items: Build a sign-up form with name, email, a country dropdown and a checkbox “I agree”. Use one state object and one change handler.
Disable the Submit button until the box is ticked.
On submit, check that the name is not empty and the email has an `@`. Show an error message next to the field.
After a good submit, show “Thanks, NAME!” and clear the form.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Every field can be typed in, and the page shows the changes at once.
Errors appear next to the field and disappear after a correct submit.
You can reach every field and the button using only the Tab key.

content.text: Summary

items: A controlled input has `value` from state and `onChange` that updates state.
Use one state object and `[name]: value` to handle many fields with one function.
Checkboxes use `checked`, selects use `value` on the select, and radios compare their value to state.
Validate on submit with clear messages, add labels, and check again on the server.

faqs.q: What is a controlled input?
faqs.a: An input whose value comes from React state and whose changes are saved to state through onChange. The state is the single source of truth.

faqs.q: Why can I not type in my input?
faqs.a: You probably set value without onChange. The input shows the fixed value from state. Add an onChange that updates the state.

faqs.q: Should I use a form library?
faqs.a: For small forms, state is enough. For large forms with many rules, a library like React Hook Form can save time. Learn the basics first.

faqs.q: Why does React warn about controlled and uncontrolled inputs?
faqs.a: The value started as undefined and later became a string. Start with an empty string so the input is controlled from the start.

lessons.title: Styling React Apps: CSS, CSS Modules, Inline Styles and Tailwind
lessons.description: Compare plain CSS, CSS Modules, inline styles and Tailwind. Make pages that fit phones and support dark mode.

content.text: A page that works but looks bad is not a good page. React does not force one way to style. You choose. In this lesson we look at the four most common ways, and when each one is best. We also learn how to change styles when state changes, how to make a page work on phones, and how to add dark mode.
Way 1: a plain CSS file
The simplest way. Write a normal CSS file, import it, and use `className` on your elements.

This works well for small projects. The weakness: CSS is **global**. A `.btn` rule affects every `.btn` in the whole app, even in other files. In a big project two people can use the same class name by accident, and styles clash.
Way 2: CSS Modules
CSS Modules fix the clash. Name your file with `.module.css`. Vite then changes each class name to a unique one, so the style only applies where you import it.
`styles` is an object, and `styles.card` is the unique class name. You write normal CSS, and you get safety for free. This is a very good default for apps of any size.
Way 3: inline styles
You met these in the JSX lesson. The `style` prop takes an object with camelCase names.
<div style={{ width: progress + '%', background: 'seagreen', height: 8 }} />

Inline styles are best for values that **change often** or come from data, like the width of a progress bar. They cannot do hover effects, media queries or other pseudo-classes, so do not use them for everything.
Way 4: Tailwind CSS

Tailwind is a popular tool that gives you many small ready-made classes, such as `p-4` (padding) and `text-lg` (large text). You build a design by putting the classes right in your JSX, and you rarely write a CSS file.

Many people like Tailwind because it is fast to work with and keeps design consistent. Others find long class lists hard to read. Both views are fair. To add it to a Vite project, follow the install guide on the Tailwind website, since the steps change between versions.
Which one should you choose?

items: **Learning and small projects:** plain CSS or CSS Modules.
**Team apps that must not clash:** CSS Modules.
**Fast building with a consistent look:** Tailwind.
**Values from data (widths, colours):** a small inline style on top of any of the above.

content.text: You can mix them. Many projects use Tailwind for most things, and an inline style for one special value. The most important thing is to be consistent inside one project.
Changing styles with state
Styles are just strings in `className`, so you can change them with state and a ternary:
With several conditions the string gets messy. A tiny helper called `clsx` joins class names and ignores false values:

import clsx from 'clsx';

<button className={clsx('btn', isPrimary && 'btn-primary', disabled && 'btn-disabled')}>
  Save
</button>
Responsive design: mobile first
Many visitors use a phone. Write the styles for a small screen first, then add rules for bigger screens with `min-width` media queries.

In Tailwind the same idea is written with prefixes: `grid grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3`. Test your page by making the browser window narrow, or use the device mode in the browser tools. Make sure nothing makes the page scroll sideways at a width of about 390 pixels.

items: Use relative sizes (`rem`, `%`, `fr`) rather than fixed pixel widths for layout.
Set `max-width: 100%` on images so they never overflow.
Make tap targets, such as buttons, at least about 44 pixels high.

content.text: Dark mode
Many devices let people choose a dark theme. You can follow that choice with one media query and CSS variables:
CSS variables (custom properties) are very useful. You change colours in one place, and the whole app follows. Always check colour contrast, so text is easy to read in both themes.
Helpful habits

items: Keep one global file for the basics: fonts, colours as variables, and a simple reset.
Put component styles next to the component, for example `Card.jsx` and `Card.module.css`.
Do not use `!important` unless you have no other choice.
Do not hide the keyboard focus outline. If you change it, make it clearly visible.
Use semantic HTML (`button`, `nav`, `main`) first, and style it second.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Using `class` instead of `className`.
Importing a CSS Module but writing a plain string: `className="card"` instead of `className={styles.card}`.
Expecting a plain CSS file to be limited to one component. It is global.
Using fixed pixel widths that break on phones.
Using inline styles for hover effects, which they cannot do.

content.text: A small example that uses everything
Here is a pricing card that is responsive, has a state-based style and supports dark mode through CSS variables. The CSS file uses a CSS Module:

The card uses CSS variables for its colours, so dark mode needs no extra code in the component. The `featured` style is added only when the prop is true. And because it is a CSS Module, the class names cannot clash with any other file. This is a good pattern to copy in your own projects.
Questions beginners often ask
**Do I have to choose only one way?** No. Many projects mix them, for example Tailwind for layout and a small CSS file for a special animation. Just keep it consistent so other people can follow it.

**Why does my CSS Module class not work?** Check that the file ends with `.module.css`, that you imported it as an object, and that you wrote `styles.name` and not a string. Class names with dashes need brackets: `styles["my-class"]`.
**How can I use a font?** Add the font files or a link in `index.html`, and set `font-family` on `body` in your global CSS. Always set a fallback font, such as `system-ui, sans-serif`.
**How do I add animation?** Start with plain CSS transitions, like `transition: background 0.2s`, for hover and focus changes. Respect people who ask for less motion with `prefers-reduced-motion`.
Your task

items: Make a `Card` component styled with a CSS Module: border, padding, rounded corners.
Make a `Tab` row of three buttons where the clicked tab is highlighted using state.
Make a grid of six cards that shows one column on a phone and three on a wide screen.
Add dark mode with CSS variables and check the text is easy to read in both themes.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: No sideways scrolling at 390 pixels wide.
The chosen tab changes colour when clicked.
Switching your device to dark mode changes the page colours.

content.text: Summary

items: Four ways to style: plain CSS, CSS Modules, inline styles and Tailwind. Pick one main way per project.
CSS Modules give each component its own class names, so styles never clash.
Use state and a ternary (or `clsx`) to change classes. Use inline styles only for values from data.
Design for phones first, use CSS variables, and support dark mode.

faqs.q: Which way of styling is best in React?
faqs.a: There is no single best. CSS Modules are a safe default, and Tailwind is popular for fast building. Choose one main way for a project and stay consistent.

faqs.q: Why does my CSS affect other components?
faqs.a: A normal CSS file is global. Use CSS Modules, or use more specific class names, to keep styles inside one component.

faqs.q: Can I use Sass or other tools?
faqs.a: Yes. Vite supports Sass after you install it. The ideas in this lesson work the same.

faqs.q: How do I test that my page works on phones?
faqs.a: Narrow your browser window, or use the device mode in your browser tools, and check there is no sideways scrolling around 390 pixels wide.
