lessons.title: React useEffect Explained: Side Effects, Dependencies and Cleanup
lessons.description: Understand useEffect in plain words: side effects, the dependency array, cleanup, and when you do not need it.

content.text: A component's main job is to describe the screen from its props and state. But sometimes a component must also do something **outside** that job: talk to a server, set a timer, listen to the window size, or change the page title. These actions are called **side effects**. React gives us the `useEffect` hook for them. It is one of the hooks people find hardest, so we go slowly, with a clear mental picture.
What is a side effect?

A side effect is anything a component does that reaches outside its own drawing work. Drawing (rendering) must be pure: the same props and state must always give the same JSX, and drawing must not change anything else. Examples of side effects:

items: Fetching data from a server.
Setting a timer with `setTimeout` or `setInterval`.
Adding an event listener to the `window`.
Changing `document.title`.
Saving something in `localStorage`.
Connecting to a chat server (a WebSocket).

content.text: You must not do these directly in the body of your component, because the body runs on every draw. Imagine fetching data in the body: the fetch would run on every draw, and when the data arrives you set state, which causes another draw, which fetches again, which loops forever. `useEffect` lets you say: “do this **after** the screen is drawn, and only when needed”.
Your first effect

`useEffect` takes a function. React draws the component first, puts it on the screen, and **then** runs your function. Here the title of the browser tab changes after each draw. This is the shape of every effect: a function that React calls after drawing.
The dependency array
As written, that effect runs after **every** draw. Often that is too much. The second argument, the **dependency array**, tells React when to run it again.

useEffect(() => { /* A */ });                 // after every draw
useEffect(() => { /* B */ }, []);             // only once, after the first draw
useEffect(() => { /* C */ }, [userId]);       // after the first draw, and again when userId changes
Think of the array as the list of things the effect **uses**. If any item in the list is different from last time, React runs the effect again. If none changed, React skips it.

items: **No array:** run after every draw. Rarely what you want.
**Empty array `[]`:** run once when the component first appears (it “mounts”).
**With values:** run on the first draw, and again whenever one of the values changes.

content.text: The rule is simple: put in the array **every prop, state and variable from your component that the effect uses**. The ESLint plugin for React hooks checks this for you and warns when something is missing. Do not turn the warning off. If you lie about the dependencies, the effect can use old values and cause bugs that are hard to find.
An effect that fetches data

When the component first appears, it fetches user number 1. If the parent later passes `userId` 2, the array has a new value, so React runs the effect again and loads user 2. The next lesson shows a complete and safe version of this, with errors and cancelling.
Cleanup: stop what you started

Some effects start something that keeps running: a timer, a listener, a connection. If you never stop it, you get a **leak**: timers pile up and old listeners keep running after the component is gone. To stop it, return a **cleanup function** from the effect. React calls it before running the effect again, and when the component is removed.

When `Clock` appears, the interval starts. When `Clock` is removed from the page, React calls the returned function, and the interval stops. Without the cleanup, the timer would try to change the state of a component that no longer exists.
The order of events
It helps to picture what React does in order for the effect with the `userId` dependency:

items: The component draws for the first time. React shows it on the screen.
React runs the effect function.
Later, `userId` changes, and the component draws again.
Before running the effect again, React runs the **cleanup** of the previous effect.
React runs the effect again with the new value.
When the component is removed, React runs the last cleanup.

content.text: Why does my effect run twice in development?

In development, `StrictMode` (which you saw in `main.jsx`) deliberately runs each effect, its cleanup and the effect again, once, right after the component first appears. It looks strange, but it is a helpful test: it checks that your cleanup really undoes your effect. If your effect works with this extra round, it will also work when a component appears and disappears many times in real life. This extra run only happens in development and never in the built site.
You might not need an effect
Effects are overused by beginners. Many things people put in an effect have a simpler way:

items: **Calculating a value from props or state:** just calculate it while drawing. `const total = price * quantity;` needs no effect and no extra state.
**Reacting to a click:** put the code in the event handler, not in an effect that watches state.
**Resetting state when a prop changes:** give the component a different `key`, and React will make a fresh one.
**Sending data after a form submit:** do it in the submit handler.

content.text: Use an effect only to **synchronise with something outside React**: the network, the browser, a timer, a library. If you are only moving data between your own state and props, you probably do not need one.
Common mistakes

items: **Missing dependency array:** the effect runs after every draw, and if it sets state it can loop forever.
**Lying about dependencies:** leaving out a value the effect uses, which gives old data.
**Forgetting cleanup** for timers, listeners and connections.
**Making the effect function `async`:** an effect must return nothing or a cleanup function, but an async function returns a promise. Put an async function inside the effect and call it.
**Using an effect for something that can be calculated** while drawing.

content.text: Your task

items: Make a component that shows the current window width and cleans up its listener.
Make a timer that counts seconds and stops when you hide it with a button.
Change the page title to show the number of items in a to-do list.
Open the browser console, add a `console.log` in the effect and its cleanup, and watch the order.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The timer stops when the component is removed (no more logs).
The window width updates as you resize the browser.
You can say in one sentence what each of the three dependency array forms does.

content.text: Summary

items: `useEffect` runs code after the screen is drawn, for work outside React such as fetching, timers and listeners.
The dependency array decides when it runs again: none means every draw, `[]` means once, values mean when they change.
Return a cleanup function to stop timers and remove listeners.
Do not use an effect for things you can calculate, or for reacting to clicks.

faqs.q: What is the dependency array in useEffect?
faqs.a: It is a list of values the effect uses. React runs the effect again only when one of them has changed since the last draw.

faqs.q: Why does useEffect run twice?
faqs.a: In development StrictMode runs effects, cleanup and effects again once to check that your cleanup works. It does not happen in the real built site.

faqs.q: Can the effect function be async?
faqs.a: No. Define an async function inside the effect and call it, because an effect must return nothing or a cleanup function.

faqs.q: When should I not use useEffect?
faqs.a: When you can calculate a value while drawing, or when the code belongs in an event handler such as a click or a form submit.

steps.say: React draws your component and puts it on the screen first.
Then it runs your effect, for example to fetch data or start a timer.
On the next draw React checks the dependency array. If nothing changed, it skips the effect.
If a dependency changed, React first runs the cleanup of the old effect, then the effect again.
When the component is removed, the last cleanup runs, so timers and listeners never leak.

lessons.title: Fetching Data in React: fetch, Loading, Errors and Cancelling Requests
lessons.description: Load data from an API safely. Show loading and error messages, cancel old requests and send data with POST.

content.text: Almost every real app talks to a server. A shop loads products, a news site loads articles, a dashboard loads numbers. In this lesson you will learn how to load data in React in a way that is safe: you will show a loading message, handle errors, and avoid a few bugs that catch many people.
The fetch function
`fetch` is built into the browser. It sends a request and gives back a **promise**, a placeholder for a result that arrives later. You wait for it with `await` inside an `async` function.

items: `fetch(url)` starts the request.
`response.ok` is true for success statuses (200 to 299). **`fetch` does not throw on a 404 or 500.** It only throws when the network itself fails. So you must check `response.ok` yourself.
`response.json()` reads the body and turns the JSON text into JavaScript data. It is also a promise, so we `await` it.

content.text: The three states of a request
While waiting, a component is in one of three situations: **loading**, **error** or **success**. Keep one piece of state for each of the first two, and one for the data:

Read it slowly. We start with `loading` true. Inside `try` we fetch and check the status. If anything fails, `catch` sets a friendly message (do not show raw technical errors to visitors). `finally` runs in both cases and turns off loading. Then, below, we use early returns, as the conditional rendering lesson showed, so each screen is clear.
The old response problem (race condition)

Imagine a page that loads user data when `userId` changes. The person clicks user 1, then quickly user 2. Two requests are in flight. If the answer for user 1 arrives **after** the answer for user 2, the page shows user 1's data while the heading says user 2. This is a **race condition**, and it is a real bug in real apps.
The fix is to use the cleanup function of the effect to cancel the old request. The browser gives us `AbortController` for this:

When `userId` changes, React runs the cleanup first, which calls `controller.abort()`. The old request stops, and `fetch` throws an `AbortError`. We ignore that special error because it is not a real problem. Only the newest request can set the state. This small pattern makes your data loading safe.
This is also what makes `StrictMode` happy: the double run in development starts a request, cancels it, and starts it again. With cleanup, nothing breaks.
Sending data with POST
To create something on a server, send a POST request with a JSON body. Do this in an event handler (such as form submit), not in an effect:

items: `method: 'POST'` says we are creating.
The `Content-Type` header tells the server the body is JSON.
`JSON.stringify` turns your JavaScript object into JSON text.
A `saving` state lets you disable the button, so people cannot click twice.

content.text: Put the logic in one helper
If every component repeats `fetch`, headers and error checks, you get a lot of copied code. Write a small helper once:

Now each component can focus on its screen. Later you can add things like a login token in one place. In lesson 25 you will meet a library, TanStack Query, that does loading, errors, caching and refreshing for you, and you will see how much code it saves.
Good habits

items: Always show a loading state, an error state and an empty state.
Show friendly messages to people, and write the technical details to the console.
Cancel or ignore old requests when inputs change.
Never put secret keys in React code. Everything in the browser can be read by visitors. Keep secrets on a server.
For text search, wait until the person stops typing (debounce) before sending a request. Lesson 21 shows how.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Not checking `response.ok` and then trying to read a 404 page as data.
Making the effect function `async` directly.
Forgetting the dependency array, so the fetch runs after every draw in a loop.
No loading state, so the page flashes or shows an empty list that looks like “no data”.
Forgetting `JSON.stringify` and the `Content-Type` header for POST.

content.text: A checklist for every screen that loads data
Before you call a data screen finished, walk through this short list. It catches most of the problems people find in real apps.

items: **First load:** does the person see a loading message, and not a blank page?
**Success:** is the data shown, and do the keys and empty cases work?
**Failure:** turn off your internet or break the URL. Is there a clear message and a way to try again?
**Slow network:** use throttling in the browser tools. Does the page still look right?
**Quick changes:** click between items quickly. Does the page always end on the item you clicked last?
**Leaving the page:** does the request stop, or at least not cause an error in the console?

content.text: If every answer is yes, your screen is in good shape. Libraries such as TanStack Query (lesson 25) give you most of these answers for free, but you now understand what they do for you.
Questions beginners often ask
**Why does my request run twice in development?** StrictMode runs effects twice on purpose. With the cleanup that cancels the old request, nothing breaks. It does not happen in the built site.
**Where should I keep the API address?** In an environment variable, such as `VITE_API_URL`, so you can change it between your computer and the live site without editing code.
**What about sending a login token?** Add it in your `api` helper, in one place, as a header such as `Authorization`. Do not copy it into every component, and never print it in logs.

**How do I refresh data after saving?** After a successful POST, either add the new item to state, or call your loading function again. Libraries such as TanStack Query do this with one call, as lesson 25 shows.
Your task

items: Load five posts from the sample API above and show Loading, an error message and the list.
Break the URL on purpose and check that your error message shows.
Add a button that loads the next five posts, and make sure old responses cannot overwrite new ones.
Create a small `api` helper and use it in your component.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You see Loading first, then the posts.
A wrong URL shows your friendly error and not a crash.
Clicking the button quickly never shows posts in the wrong order.

content.text: Summary

items: Use `fetch` inside an effect (or an event handler for POST). Check `response.ok`, because fetch does not throw on 404 or 500.
Keep loading, error and data state, and show each one clearly.
Use `AbortController` and the effect cleanup to avoid showing old responses.
Put repeated fetch code in one helper, and never put secrets in React code.

faqs.q: Why does fetch not throw an error for a 404?
faqs.a: Fetch only fails when the network fails. A 404 or 500 is still a valid response, so you must check response.ok yourself.

faqs.q: What is a race condition in data fetching?
faqs.a: Two requests are sent, and the older one finishes last, so old data replaces new data. Cancel old requests with AbortController to avoid it.

faqs.q: Should I use axios instead of fetch?
faqs.a: Fetch is built in and enough for most apps. Axios adds some convenience, but you do not need it. Learn fetch first.

faqs.q: Where should I call fetch: in an effect or an event handler?
faqs.a: Use an effect to load data when a component appears or its inputs change. Use an event handler for actions such as submitting a form.

lessons.title: React useRef Explained: Access the DOM and Keep Values Without Redrawing
lessons.description: Learn useRef: focus an input, scroll to an element, keep a timer id, and know when to use a ref and not state.

content.text: State is for data that the screen shows. But sometimes you need to remember something that the screen does **not** show, or reach a real element on the page. For these cases, React gives you `useRef`. It is small, but very useful once you understand it.
What is a ref?
A **ref** is a box that holds a value. You make one with `useRef(initialValue)`. It returns an object with a single field, `current`, that holds the value.
Two facts make refs special:

items: React **keeps** the ref between draws, so the value is not lost, just like state.
Changing `ref.current` does **not** make React draw the component again, unlike state.

content.text: So a ref is like a private notebook: you can write in it and read from it, but writing does not tell the screen to change.
Use 1: focus an input
The most common use is to reach a real element in the page. Give the element a `ref` prop. After the element is drawn, React puts it in `ref.current`.

Before the first draw, `inputRef.current` is `null`. After the page is drawn, it points to the real input element, so you can call browser methods such as `.focus()`. You can only use it in event handlers and effects, not while drawing.
A common case: focus the first field of a form when the page opens.
Another case: when a form shows an error, move the focus to the first wrong field. That helps people who use keyboards or screen readers.
Use 2: scroll to an element
A chat window uses the same trick: after a new message is added, scroll the last message into view.
Use 3: keep a value that does not affect the screen
Some values must survive between draws, but do not change what is on the screen. A timer id is the classic example:
The `seconds` value is **state**, because the screen shows it. The `timerId` is a **ref**, because the screen does not show it, and we do not want a redraw when we set it.
Use 4: remember the previous value
The hook returns the value **from the last draw**, because the effect updates the ref only after the draw is done. This small custom hook is a nice example of a ref storing a value quietly.
Ref or state: how to choose

items: If the screen must change when the value changes, use **state**.
If you only need to remember it, or hold a real element, use a **ref**.
Never read or write `ref.current` while the component is drawing. Do it in event handlers or effects.

content.text: A very common mistake is to use a ref to avoid a redraw when the data really is shown on the screen. Then the screen goes out of date. If the person can see it, it should be state.
Refs and other components
A ref on your own component does not work the same way as on a plain element. In React 19 you can pass `ref` as a normal prop to your own components:
In older versions of React (18 and before) you had to wrap the component in a function called `forwardRef`. You may see that in older code. It does the same job.
Uncontrolled inputs with refs
You can read an input's value with a ref instead of keeping it in state. This is called an **uncontrolled** input. It is shorter for simple cases, because you do not redraw on every key press:
Notice `defaultValue` instead of `value`: it sets only the starting text, and the browser keeps control after that.
Common mistakes

items: Reading `ref.current` when it is still `null`, for example during the first draw. Use it in handlers and effects.
Using a ref for data that the screen shows, so the screen does not update.
Forgetting `.current`. The ref is an object. The value is in `ref.current`.
Writing to `ref.current` while drawing. It makes the component unpredictable.
Using refs to change the page in ways React should handle. Prefer state for anything that changes what is drawn.

content.text: A worked example: a chat box
Here is a small chat that uses a ref twice: to scroll to the newest message, and to put the cursor back in the input after sending.

The messages and the text are **state**, because the screen shows them. The two refs only point at real elements, so we can call browser methods on them. After each new message the effect scrolls an empty `div` at the bottom into view. After sending, the input gets focus again, so the person can keep typing without clicking. This is a good picture of the right split: state for what is shown, refs for reaching into the page.
Questions beginners often ask
**Can I have many refs in one component?** Yes. Make one `useRef` for each thing you need. For a list of items you can store the elements in an object inside one ref, or use a ref callback.

**Is it wrong to change the page directly with a ref?** For small things like focus and scrolling it is fine. Avoid using refs to change what is drawn, such as text or classes, because React will not know and may overwrite your changes. Use state for that.
**Does changing a ref cause a render?** No, and that is the point. If you need the screen to update, use state instead.
Your task

items: Make a form that focuses the name field when the page opens.
Make a button that scrolls smoothly to a section at the bottom of the page.
Make a stopwatch with Start, Stop and Reset buttons using a ref for the timer id.
Show the previous value of a counter using `usePrevious`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The cursor is in the name field when the page opens.
The stopwatch stops when you press Stop and does not run twice when you press Start twice.
No timers keep running after the component is removed.

content.text: Summary

items: `useRef(initial)` gives an object with `current`. React keeps it between draws, and changing it does not cause a redraw.
Put a ref on an element to get the real DOM node, for example to focus it or scroll it into view.
Use refs for timer ids, previous values and other things the screen does not show.
If the screen shows it, use state, not a ref.

faqs.q: What is the difference between useRef and useState?
faqs.a: Changing state makes the component draw again. Changing a ref does not. Use state for data the screen shows, and a ref for values you only need to remember.

faqs.q: Why is ref.current null?
faqs.a: The element has not been drawn yet. Refs are filled after the first draw, so use them inside event handlers or effects.

faqs.q: What is forwardRef?
faqs.a: In React 18 and older, it was the way to pass a ref through your own component. In React 19, you can pass ref as a normal prop.

faqs.q: Should I use refs to read form values?
faqs.a: You can, for simple forms. This is called uncontrolled input. For forms that check values as people type, controlled inputs with state are easier.

lessons.title: Lifting State Up and Component Composition in React
lessons.description: Learn where state should live, how two components share data through a parent, and how children avoid prop drilling.

content.text: As an app grows, you meet a new question: **where should this state live?** Two components far apart might need the same data. This lesson shows the simple rule that answers most of these questions, and a second idea, composition, that keeps your code clean.
The problem: two components, one value

Imagine a page with a temperature input in Celsius and a display of the same temperature in Fahrenheit. Each is a separate component. They both need the same number. If each keeps its own state, they will disagree. The numbers must come from **one place**.
Lifting state up

The rule: **move the state to the closest parent that is shared by the components that need it**. The parent keeps the state and passes the value down with props. When a child wants to change it, the parent also passes down a function.

The state lives in `TemperatureApp`. `CelsiusInput` has no state of its own: it shows the `value` it is given, and calls `onChange` when the person types. `FahrenheitDisplay` calculates its answer from the same number. Because there is only one copy of the data, the two parts can never disagree. This is called **a single source of truth**.
Also notice that `fahrenheit` is not state. It is calculated from `celsius`. Do not store in state what you can calculate.
Data down, events up
This is the basic rhythm of React:

items: **Data goes down:** parents pass values to children as props.
**Events go up:** children call functions given by the parent, and the parent changes its state.

content.text: It keeps the app easy to follow. When a value looks wrong, you look at the component that owns the state. There is only one place to check.
How high should state go?

Not too high, not too low. Keep state as **close to where it is used** as you can, and lift it only when two or more components really need it. If you put everything at the top, every small change redraws a lot and the code is hard to read. A good test: ask “who needs to know this?”, and find the lowest component that is a parent of all of them.
The problem of passing props down many levels
Sometimes the component that needs the data is deep in the tree. You end up passing a prop through many components that do not use it, only to hand it on. People call this **prop drilling**.

<Page user={user}>
  <Header user={user}>
    <Menu user={user}>
      <Avatar user={user} />   {/* only Avatar uses it */}
    </Menu>
  </Header>
</Page>
For two or three levels this is fine and clear. For many levels there are two good fixes. The first is **composition**, shown next. The second is **context**, which lesson 16 covers.
Composition: pass components as children
Instead of passing data down through the middle layers, build the part that needs the data at the top, and pass it **as children or as a prop**. The middle layers then do not need to know about it.
`Page` has the data and builds `Avatar` itself. `Layout` and `Header` only place whatever they are given. No prop drilling, and these components become more reusable, because they can hold anything.

This idea, **composition over configuration**, is a very React way to think. Instead of a component with many options (`showIcon`, `iconPosition`, `iconColor`), give it a place where you can put anything:
Moving state back down

Sometimes a part of the state is only used by one child, but was lifted to a parent too early. Moving it back down makes the parent simpler. Example: the text in a search box is used only by the search box, until you press Search. Keep the text inside the box, and only send the final text up on submit.
Derived data and a single source of truth

items: Keep **minimal state**: the smallest set of values that describes the situation.
Calculate everything else while drawing: totals, filtered lists, counts, labels.
Never keep the same fact in two places. Copies drift apart. If two components need it, they get it from one owner.

content.text: A worked example: a shopping page

A shop page has a product list and a cart summary in the header. Both depend on the same cart. The page component owns the cart state, passes the cart to the header (to show the count), and passes an `onAdd` function to each product. When someone clicks Add on a product, the product calls `onAdd(product)`. The page adds the product to the cart with a new array. React draws again, and the header shows the new count. No component keeps its own copy of the cart. You will build this in the task below.
Common mistakes

items: Keeping the same value in two components, so they show different numbers.
Lifting state too high, so the whole page redraws for a small change.
Forgetting to pass the handler down, so the child cannot change the parent.
Storing derived data in state, such as a count or a filtered list.
Passing the setter itself to deep children everywhere instead of a clear `onSomething` function.

content.text: A quick way to decide where state lives
When you are unsure, ask these three questions in order. They give a clear answer most of the time.

items: **Which components use this data?** Write them down, even if there is only one.
**What is their closest common parent?** Look at your component tree and find the lowest component that contains all of them.
**Is that parent too far up?** If the answer is a very high component, check whether you can restructure with composition, or whether the data is really shared app-wide, which suits context.

content.text: If only one component uses the data, keep the state inside it. If two siblings use it, put it in their parent. If many components in different branches use it, think about context. Following these steps stops two common problems: state kept too high, so the whole page redraws, and state copied in two places, so the numbers disagree.
Your task

items: Build the temperature example above and add a Kelvin display.
Build a small shop: a list of three products, each with an Add button, and a header showing how many items are in the cart. Keep the cart state in the page.
Add a `Panel` component with `title`, `actions` and `children`, and use it twice.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: All displays change together when the input changes.
The cart count in the header always matches the items added.
No state is stored that could be calculated.

content.text: Summary

items: When two components need the same state, move it to their closest shared parent. This keeps one source of truth.
Data goes down with props. Events go up with function props.
Keep state minimal and calculate the rest while drawing.
Use composition (`children` and component props) to avoid long chains of props.

faqs.q: What does lifting state up mean?
faqs.a: Moving the state from a child to the closest parent that is shared by all the components that need it, and passing it down with props.

faqs.q: What is prop drilling?
faqs.a: Passing props through many levels of components that do not use them, only to reach a deep child. Composition or context can fix it.

faqs.q: When should I use composition instead of context?
faqs.a: Try composition first. Pass components as children or props from the top. Use context when many components at different depths really need the same data.

faqs.q: Where should state live?
faqs.a: As low as possible, but high enough that every component that needs it can reach it through a shared parent.

lessons.title: React useReducer Explained: Manage Complex State with Actions
lessons.description: Learn useReducer with a to-do list. Understand actions, reducers and when to choose it over useState.

content.text: `useState` is perfect for simple values. But when a component has many pieces of state that change together, or many ways to change them, the code can become messy. The `useReducer` hook gives you a tidy way to organise it. It is a favourite for complex state, and it is also the idea behind Redux, which you will meet later.
The problem: too many setters
Look at a to-do list that can add, toggle, delete and clear finished tasks. With `useState`, handlers each have their own logic spread around the component:
This is fine for four. For fifteen kinds of changes, or when the state has many fields, it is hard to see all the rules in one place. `useReducer` moves all of the rules into **one function**.
The idea: actions and a reducer

items: An **action** is a small object that describes **what happened**, for example `{ type: 'added', text: 'Buy milk' }`. It does not change anything. It is a message.
A **reducer** is a function that takes the **current state** and an **action**, and returns the **new state**. All of the rules are in it.
`dispatch` is the function you call to send an action to the reducer.

content.text: You can think of it like a shop: customers (your components) do not walk to the shelves and change the stock. They hand a note (an action) to the shopkeeper (the reducer), who updates the stock by the rules.
A first example: the counter

`useReducer(reducer, initialState)` returns the current state and `dispatch`. When you call `dispatch({ type: 'increment' })`, React calls `reducer(currentState, thatAction)` and uses the returned object as the new state, then draws again. The `switch` lists every way the state can change, in one readable place.
The rules of a reducer

items: **It must be pure:** the same state and action always give the same result. No fetching, no random numbers, no changing outside things inside it.
**It must not change the old state.** Return a **new** object or array. Copy with spread, `map` and `filter`, just as in the state lessons.
**Always return something.** If an action is not known, throw an error or return the old state.

content.text: A real example: a to-do list

The component only says **what happened** (`added`, `toggled`, `deleted`). It does not know how the list changes. All the rules live in `tasksReducer`. You can read that one function and understand every change. You can even move it to its own file and test it without React, because it is a plain function.

Notice that the form text uses a normal `useState`. You can mix them: use `useState` for simple, local values and `useReducer` for the state with many rules. The id is made **before** dispatching, because a reducer must be pure and cannot make random ids itself.
Action names

Name actions after **what happened**, in the past tense: `'added'`, `'deleted'`, `'form_submitted'`, rather than commands like `'setTasks'`. This keeps the reducer about events and makes logs easy to read. You may send extra data in the action, such as `id` or `text`, often named `payload`.
useState or useReducer?

items: **useState** is shorter for simple, independent values: a toggle, a text box, a counter.
**useReducer** shines when the next state depends on the old one in several ways, when state has many related fields, or when you want all the rules in one place that is easy to test.
**Start with useState.** Move to `useReducer` when your handlers start to look like a pile of rules.

content.text: A bonus: when many deep components need to change the state, you can pass `dispatch` down instead of many handler functions. React keeps `dispatch` the same between draws, so it is also safe in effects. Together with context (lesson 16), `useReducer` gives you a small state manager without any library.
A form state example

Here the form has values, a status and an error that change together. With four named actions, each step of the form is easy to read: a field changed, sending started, sending failed, sending worked. The status can be `idle`, `sending` or `done`, so there are no impossible combinations like “loading” and “done” both true.
Common mistakes

items: Changing the state inside the reducer (`state.count++` or `tasks.push(...)`). Return a new value.
Making ids or calling `fetch` inside the reducer. Do those before dispatching.
Forgetting a `return` in a case, so the new state becomes `undefined`.
Writing actions as commands that hide meaning, such as `'set'`.
Using `useReducer` for a single toggle, which is more code than needed.

content.text: Following one dispatch
Let us follow a single click through the to-do reducer so that nothing feels hidden. The person ticks the box of the task with id 7.

items: The checkbox calls `dispatch({ type: 'toggled', id: 7 })`.
React calls `tasksReducer(currentTasks, { type: 'toggled', id: 7 })`.
The reducer finds the `'toggled'` case. It goes through the list with `map`, and for the task with id 7 it returns a **new object** with `done` flipped. All other tasks are returned as they are.
The reducer returns a **new array**. React sees that the state is a different object, and draws the component again.
The list is drawn from the new array, and the box for task 7 shows as ticked.

content.text: The component never needed to know how toggling works. If you later decide that ticking a task should also record the time it was finished, you change one case in the reducer, and nothing else. That is the real benefit: the rules live in one place.
Your task

items: Build the counter with a `step` field, and an action `'step_changed'`.
Build the to-do list above, and add an action `'edited'` that changes the text of a task.
Build a shopping cart reducer with actions `'added'`, `'quantity_changed'` and `'removed'`, and show the total price.
Write the reducer in a separate file and test it with a few plain function calls in the console.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The list stays correct after any mix of actions.
The reducer never changes the old state (you always return a new array or object).
You can find every possible change of the state in one function.

content.text: Summary

items: `useReducer(reducer, initial)` gives `[state, dispatch]`. Call `dispatch(action)` and React runs the reducer to get the new state.
An action describes what happened. A reducer is a pure function `(state, action) => newState`.
Never change old state in a reducer. Return new arrays and objects.
Start with `useState`. Use `useReducer` when state logic becomes complex.

faqs.q: When should I use useReducer instead of useState?
faqs.a: When the state has many related fields or many kinds of updates, and you want all the rules in one place that is easy to read and test. For simple values, useState is shorter.

faqs.q: What is an action?
faqs.a: A small object that describes what happened, such as { type: "added", text: "Buy milk" }. It is sent to the reducer with dispatch.

faqs.q: Why must a reducer be pure?
faqs.a: React may call it more than once and expects the same result for the same input. Doing outside work inside it, like fetching, makes it unpredictable.

faqs.q: Is useReducer the same as Redux?
faqs.a: The idea is the same: actions and a reducer. Redux adds a global store, tools and extra features for large apps. useReducer works inside one component tree.

lessons.title: React Context API Explained: Share Data Without Passing Props
lessons.description: Share data like the theme or user without passing props. Learn createContext, Provider and useContext with examples.

content.text: In the lifting state lesson we met **prop drilling**: passing data through many components that do not use it. Context is React's built-in way to make some data available to **any** component below a certain point, without passing props through every level. Think of it as a shared board in a building that every room can read.
When is context a good choice?
Use context for data that many components at different levels need, and that does not change very often. Typical examples:

items: The **current user** who is signed in.
The **theme**: light or dark.
The chosen **language**.
A **shopping cart** used by the header, the product pages and the checkout.

content.text: Do not use context for everything. If only a parent and child need a value, props are simpler and clearer.
The three steps

items: **Create** the context with `createContext(defaultValue)`.
**Provide** a value with `<Context.Provider value={...}>` around the part of the page that needs it.
**Use** the value in any component below with `useContext(Context)`.

content.text: Example: a theme
First we create the context, in its own file:

`ThemeProvider` is a normal component that keeps the theme in state and shares it. `children` is whatever you put inside it. We also export a small helper, `useTheme`, so other components do not need to know about `useContext` or the context object. It is a custom hook, which lesson 17 explains.
Next we wrap the app once, near the top:
Now any component, at any depth, can read the theme:
No props travel through the layers between. When `toggleTheme` runs, the provider's state changes, and every component that uses the context draws again with the new value.
Example: the signed-in user
The check in `useAuth` is a helpful habit. If you forget to wrap your app in the provider, you get a clear error message instead of a confusing `undefined`.
How context finds its value

`useContext` looks **up** the tree for the nearest provider of that context. You can even put a provider inside another one to change the value for one part of the page only. If there is no provider above, you get the **default value** from `createContext(defaultValue)`.
A performance warning

When the value in a provider changes, **every component that reads that context draws again**. In the examples above we wrote `value={{ theme, toggleTheme }}`, which makes a new object on every draw of the provider, so all readers redraw even when nothing really changed. For small apps this is fine. In bigger apps you can keep the value steady with `useMemo`, which lesson 21 covers:

const value = useMemo(() => ({ user, login, logout }), [user]);
return <AuthContext.Provider value={value}>{children}</AuthContext.Provider>;

items: Split big contexts: one for the user, one for the theme, one for the cart. A change in one does not redraw the readers of the others.
Keep rarely changing and often changing data in different contexts.
Put the provider as low in the tree as it can be, only around the parts that need it.

content.text: Context and useReducer together
For bigger shared state, combine them. The reducer holds the rules, and the context shares the state and `dispatch`:
This is a small, complete state manager with no extra library. For very large apps or special needs you can reach for Redux Toolkit or Zustand, which lesson 24 introduces.
Context is not a database

Context only **shares** state with components. The state itself still lives in `useState` or `useReducer` inside the provider. If you need data from a server, load it (lesson 12) and then put the result in the provider, or use a data library (lesson 25).
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting the provider, so the component gets the default value (often `null`).
Putting everything in one giant context, so every change redraws everything.
Using context for data that only one parent and child share, where props are simpler.
Making the value a new object every draw without thinking about performance in a larger app.
Trying to change a context value directly. You must call the function the provider shares, which changes the provider's state.

content.text: Following the value through the tree
It is useful to picture what happens when someone clicks the theme button. The button lives deep inside the page, and the provider is at the very top.

items: The button calls `toggleTheme`, a function that came from the context.
That function belongs to the provider, so it calls `setTheme` in the provider's own state.
The provider's state changes, so the provider renders again, and puts a new `value` into the context.
React finds every component that called `useContext` for this context, and draws them again with the new value.
Components that do not read the context are left alone, unless their parent redrew.

content.text: This shows an important point: the state still lives in an ordinary `useState`. The context is only the **delivery system** that brings the value, and the functions to change it, to every place that needs them. You can think of the provider as a small power station, and `useContext` as the plug in each room.
A rule of thumb for choosing

items: If you pass a prop through **one or two** levels, keep passing props. It is clear and simple.
If you pass the same prop through **three or more** levels that do not use it, try composition first.
If many unrelated components need the same value, such as the user or the theme, use context.

content.text: Questions beginners often ask
**Can I have more than one provider?** Yes, as many as you need. You can nest them, for example a theme provider inside an auth provider. Each context is separate.
**Where does the provider go?** Around the parts of the app that need the data. Often that is `main.jsx`, wrapped around `App`. You can also place a provider lower in the tree for one section.
**Can I change context from a child?** Yes, but through a function that the provider shares, such as `toggleTheme`. The provider owns the state, so changes go through it.
**Is context only for global data?** It is for data that many components share. It does not have to be for the whole app. A form with many parts can have a small context just for itself.
Your task

items: Build a `ThemeProvider` with a toggle button, and show the theme name in two different components.
Build an `AuthProvider` with `login` and `logout`, and show different content in a header for each case.
Make `useTheme` throw a helpful error when used outside a provider.
Create a `CartProvider` with `useReducer` and show the number of items in the header and in a cart page.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Both components change when you press the toggle.
Using the hook outside a provider shows your clear error message.
The cart count in the header always matches the cart page.

content.text: Summary

items: Context shares data with any component below a provider, with no prop drilling.
Steps: `createContext`, wrap with `Provider value={...}`, read with `useContext`.
Wrap the context in a custom hook, and check that a provider exists.
A changed value redraws every reader. Split contexts and keep values steady in big apps.

faqs.q: What is the React Context API used for?
faqs.a: To share data such as the user, theme or language with many components at different levels, without passing props through every level.

faqs.q: Does context replace Redux?
faqs.a: For small and medium apps, context with useReducer is often enough. Redux and similar libraries add tools and optimisations that help in large apps.

faqs.q: Why do all my components redraw when context changes?
faqs.a: Every component that reads a context draws again when its value changes. Split big contexts into smaller ones, and keep the value steady.

faqs.q: Where should I put the provider?
faqs.a: Around the smallest part of the tree that needs the data. Often that is the top of the app, for things like the user and theme.

lessons.title: React Custom Hooks: Reuse Logic Between Components
lessons.description: Write your own hooks: useToggle, useLocalStorage, useFetch and useDebounce. Reuse logic in many components.

content.text: You already use hooks that React gives you: `useState`, `useEffect` and others. React also lets you make **your own hooks**. A custom hook is a normal JavaScript function that uses other hooks and lets you **reuse logic** in many components. Components share their screens, and custom hooks share their behaviour.
What is a custom hook?

A custom hook is a function whose name starts with `use`, and which calls other hooks inside. That is all. The name matters: it tells React, and the lint rules, that the function follows the rules of hooks. Each component that calls a custom hook gets **its own separate copy** of the state inside it. Hooks share the logic, not the data.
Example 1: useToggle
Many components have a true or false switch: a menu, a modal, a password field. Instead of writing the same state and handler each time, write a hook once:
The hook returns an array, just like `useState`. You can return an object instead when there are many values. Choose what is easier to read for the person using the hook.
Example 2: useLocalStorage
Saving a value in the browser, so that it is still there after a reload, needs a little code that you will want in many places. Put it in a hook:

Two details to notice. First, `useState(() => ...)` takes a **function**, called **lazy initial state**. React runs it only on the first draw, so we read storage once, not on every draw. Second, `try` and `catch` protect us, because storage can be blocked, for example in private browsing. Never store passwords or private data in `localStorage`, because any script on the page can read it.
Example 3: useFetch
Loading, error and data appeared in the data lesson. Wrap them once:

The component is now only a few lines, and it still handles loading, errors and cancelling. If you later improve `useFetch`, every component gets the improvement. For big apps, a library like TanStack Query (lesson 25) gives you a more complete version of this idea.
Example 4: useDebounce
When someone types in a search box, you do not want to send a request on every key press. A **debounce** waits until the person pauses:

Each key press sets a new timer and cancels the old one with the cleanup. Only when the person stops typing for 400 milliseconds does `debounced` change, and only then does the search start. `encodeURIComponent` makes the text safe to use in a URL.
Example 5: useWindowSize and useOnline
Hooks are very good at wrapping browser features that need a listener and a cleanup:
Now any component can show a banner such as “You are offline” with a single line: `const online = useOnline();`.
The rules of hooks

items: Call hooks **only at the top level** of a component or a custom hook. Never inside `if`, loops, nested functions or after an early `return`.
Call hooks **only from React components or custom hooks**, never from normal functions.
Name custom hooks starting with `use`.

content.text: React remembers state by the **order** of the hook calls. If the order could change between draws, React would give the wrong state to the wrong hook. The ESLint plugin `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` checks these rules for you. Keep it on.
How to design a good hook

items: Give it **one clear job** and a clear name: `useDebounce`, not `useStuff`.
Accept **simple inputs** (a key, a URL, a delay) and return **simple outputs**.
Make it work for the first draw, for changes and for cleanup.
Do not make a hook just to move code around. Make one when logic repeats, or when it makes a component much easier to read.

content.text: Where to keep hooks
Put them in a `hooks` folder inside `src`, one file for each hook, named after it, for example `src/hooks/useDebounce.js`. A custom hook file needs no JSX, so `.js` is fine.
Common mistakes

items: Calling a hook inside a condition or loop.
Forgetting that each call of a hook has its own separate state, and expecting two components to share data (use context for that).
Missing cleanup for listeners and timers in the hook.
Forgetting dependencies in the effect inside the hook.
Naming the function without `use`, so the lint rules cannot help.

content.text: When to make a custom hook: a short guide
Beginners sometimes make hooks for everything, and sometimes never make one. A simple guide helps you find the right time.

items: You wrote the **same state and effect** in two places. This is the clearest sign. Move it into a hook.
A component is **long** because one piece of logic, such as a timer or a listener, takes many lines. A hook with a good name hides the details and makes the component easy to read.
The logic is something you can **name in a few words**, such as “keeps a value in storage” or “knows if the user is online”.

content.text: Do not make a hook if you only call one built-in hook and there is no real logic around it. `function useCount() { return useState(0); }` adds nothing. A hook should hide some work, not just rename a function.

A final tip: after you write a hook, use it from **two different components** to check that it works well with separate state in each. If the hook only works for one place, it is probably not general enough yet, and you may want to change its inputs.
Questions beginners often ask
**Can a custom hook return JSX?** It can, but usually it should not. A hook shares logic. If you want to share a piece of screen, make a component instead.
**Can hooks call other hooks?** Yes. This is how bigger hooks are built, for example `useSearch` can use both `useDebounce` and `useFetch`.
**How do I test a custom hook?** Use `renderHook` from React Testing Library, as lesson 26 shows. Or test it through a small component that uses it.

**Should I share hooks between projects?** Good hooks are often copied between your own projects, or published as small packages. Libraries such as `usehooks-ts` and `react-use` also give you many ready-made hooks to read and learn from.
Your task

items: Write `useToggle` and use it for a menu and for a show/hide password button.
Write `useLocalStorage` and keep a dark mode choice after reload.
Write `useDebounce` and use it for a search box that filters a local list.
Write `useOnline` and show a banner when the internet is lost (turn the network off in your browser tools to test).

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Each hook works in two components at the same time, with separate state.
The saved choice survives a reload.
Typing quickly in the search box does not filter on every key press.

content.text: Summary

items: A custom hook is a function starting with `use` that calls other hooks, so you can reuse logic.
Each call gets its own state. Hooks share logic, not data.
Good candidates: toggles, storage, fetching, debounce, browser listeners.
Follow the rules of hooks: top level only, and only in components or other hooks.

faqs.q: What is a custom hook in React?
faqs.a: A function whose name starts with use and which calls other hooks. It lets you reuse state and effect logic in many components.

faqs.q: Do two components that use the same custom hook share state?
faqs.a: No. Each component gets its own copy of the state. To share data, use context or lift state up.

faqs.q: Why must hook names start with use?
faqs.a: It tells React and the lint tools that the function follows the rules of hooks, so mistakes can be found early.

faqs.q: Is it safe to store data in localStorage?
faqs.a: It is fine for simple choices like a theme. Never store passwords or private data there, because scripts on the page can read it.

lessons.title: React Router: Multiple Pages, Links, Params, Layouts and Protected Routes
lessons.description: Build a multi-page app with React Router: routes, links, URL params, layouts, 404 page and protected routes.

content.text: A real website has many pages: home, about, product pages, a login page. A React app is made of one HTML file, so how do we show different pages? We use **React Router**, the most used routing library for React. It changes what the screen shows when the address changes, **without** reloading the page. That makes the app feel fast.
This lesson uses React Router version 6 or newer, with the `react-router-dom` package. Names and some details can change between versions, so check the official docs if something differs.
Install and set up
npm install react-router-dom
Wrap your app in a **router** once, in `main.jsx`:
`BrowserRouter` watches the address bar and tells your app when it changes.
Routes: which component for which address
Each `Route` pairs a `path` with an `element`. React Router shows the one that matches the address. The path `*` matches anything else, so it is perfect for a **404 page**. Always add one.
Links without reloading
A normal `<a href>` makes the browser load a whole new page and your state is lost. Use `Link` instead, which changes the address and shows the new page **without a reload**:
`NavLink` is a `Link` that knows when it matches the current page, so you can style the active link. For links to **other websites**, keep using a normal `<a href>`.
URL parameters
A shop has one page design for many products, such as `/products/1` and `/products/2`. Put a **parameter** in the path with a colon, and read it with `useParams`:

} /> import { useParams } from 'react-router-dom'; function ProductPage() { const { id } = useParams(); return

Product number {id}

; }
Parameters are always **strings**, so convert with `Number(id)` if you need a number. Use the id to load the right data, as in the fetching lesson.
Query strings (search parameters)

The part after a question mark, like `/products?category=books&page=2`, is the query string. It is perfect for filters, search and pages, because people can **share** and **bookmark** the exact view, and the back button works.
It works like `useState`, but the state lives in the **address**. Keeping filters in the URL, rather than in private state, is a very good habit.
Shared layouts with nested routes
Most pages share a header and a footer. Instead of repeating them, make a **layout route**. It draws the shared parts and an `Outlet`, where the matching child page appears.
The layout stays on the screen while only the content in the `Outlet` changes. The menu is not drawn again from nothing, so things like its state stay.
Moving with code: useNavigate
Sometimes you must change page from code, for example after a form is saved:

`navigate(-1)` goes back one page, like the back button. `navigate('/x', { replace: true })` replaces the current page in the history, so the back button does not return to it. That is useful after a login.
For a simple redirect while drawing, return `<Navigate to="/login" />`.
Protected routes
Some pages should be open only to signed-in people. Make a small component that checks, and redirects if needed:
If there is no user, we send the visitor to the login page and remember where they wanted to go in `state`. After login, you can send them back with `navigate(location.state?.from?.pathname || '/')`.

Hiding a page in React only changes what the browser shows. **A visitor can still read any code you send to the browser.** Your server must check permissions for the data itself. Never trust the front end alone.
Scroll and titles

items: When the page changes, the scroll position can stay where it was. Add a small component that calls `window.scrollTo(0, 0)` when `useLocation().pathname` changes.

Set a different `document.title` on each page. It helps people and search engines. A client-side React app is harder for search engines to read than normal HTML, so for pages that must rank well, think about server rendering with a framework such as Next.js.
Move focus to the main heading after a change, to help keyboard and screen reader users.

content.text: Data routers (a short note)

Newer versions of React Router also have a **data router** style, with `createBrowserRouter`, loaders and actions, which load data before showing a page. It is a good next step once you know the basics here. The ideas (routes, links, params, layouts) are the same.
Deploy note

With client-side routing, a visit directly to `/products/3` asks the **server** for that path. Your server or host must send `index.html` for unknown paths, or visitors see a 404 on reload. Most hosts have a setting for this, called “single page app fallback” or a rewrite rule.
Common mistakes

items: Using `<a href>` for inside links, which reloads the page.
Forgetting the `*` route for 404.
Forgetting to render `<Outlet />` in the layout, so child pages never appear.
Treating `useParams` values as numbers. They are strings.
Forgetting the host fallback, so a page reload gives a server 404.

content.text: A small complete app
Here is how the pieces fit together in one small file. It has a layout, three pages, a product page that reads the URL and a page for unknown addresses.

Read it from the bottom. The router watches the address. The layout draws the menu, and the `Outlet` shows the page that matches. The product page reads the id from the address and finds its data, and shows a message if the id is unknown. That last check matters: someone can type any address, so a page that uses a parameter must always handle a missing item.
Questions beginners often ask

**What is the difference between BrowserRouter and HashRouter?** `BrowserRouter` gives clean addresses like `/about` and needs the server fallback to `index.html`. `HashRouter` puts the page after a `#`, like `/#/about`, and works on any host without extra setup, but the addresses look less clean.
**How do I go back with a button?** Call `navigate(-1)`, which works like the browser back button.
**How do I highlight the current link?** Use `NavLink`. It gives you `isActive` so you can add a class or style to the link of the current page.
**Can I read the URL from a deep component?** Yes. Call `useParams`, `useLocation` or `useSearchParams` in any component under the router. There is no need to pass the values down as props.
Your task

items: Make an app with Home, About and Products pages, a shared layout with a menu, and a 404 page.
Add `/products/:id` and show the id. Link to three products.
Add a category filter that lives in the query string.
Add a fake login with context, a protected Dashboard page, and a redirect back after login.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Changing pages does not reload the browser.
Reloading on `/products/2` still works in the dev server.
Visiting the Dashboard while signed out sends you to the login page.

content.text: Summary

items: React Router shows different components for different addresses without reloading.
Use `Routes` and `Route`, `Link` and `NavLink`, `useParams`, `useSearchParams` and `useNavigate`.
Layout routes with `Outlet` share headers and footers.
Protect routes with a wrapper that redirects, and always check permissions on the server too.

faqs.q: Why use Link instead of an anchor tag?
faqs.a: Link changes the page without a full reload, so your state and speed are kept. A normal anchor makes the browser load a whole new page.

faqs.q: How do I read an id from the URL?
faqs.a: Define the route with a parameter, like /products/:id, and read it with useParams. It is always a string.

faqs.q: Why do I get a 404 when I reload a page after deploying?
faqs.a: The server looks for a real file at that path. Set up a fallback so unknown paths return index.html and let React Router show the page.

faqs.q: Are protected routes secure?
faqs.a: They only change what the browser shows. Anything sent to the browser can be read. Your server must also check permissions for the data.

lessons.title: Advanced React Forms: FormData, Validation Rules and React Hook Form
lessons.description: Go further with forms: FormData, clean validation, helpful errors, and when React Hook Form is worth using.

content.text: In lesson 9 you built forms with controlled inputs, where every key press goes through state. That is great to learn the idea, but it is not the only way, and for big forms it can be too much code. In this lesson you will learn the shorter way with `FormData`, how to write clean validation, and how a form library can help.
The browser already knows your form
A normal HTML form already keeps the values of its fields. When the person submits, the browser can hand you all values at once with `FormData`. You do not need state for every field.

items: Every input needs a **`name`**. That name becomes the key in the data.
`event.currentTarget` is the form itself.
`Object.fromEntries(formData)` turns the form data into a plain object.
There is no state at all, and no redraw while the person types.

content.text: Checkboxes with the same name give several values. Use `formData.getAll('hobby')` to read them as an array. A file input gives a `File` object, so you can send the whole `formData` to a server with `fetch(url, { method: 'POST', body: formData })`. Do not set the `Content-Type` header yourself in that case, because the browser must add the right boundary.
Use the browser's own validation first

HTML gives you free checks: `required`, `type="email"`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `min`, `max` and `pattern`. The browser shows a message and stops the submit. This is a good first layer, and it works without any JavaScript.

<input name="age" type="number" min="18" max="99" required />
<input name="code" pattern="[0-9]{6}" title="Six digits" required />
The built-in bubbles look different in each browser, and you cannot style them easily. When you need your own messages, add `noValidate` to the form and write your own checks.
Writing your own validation function
Put the rules in **one plain function** that takes the data and returns an object of errors. It is easy to read and easy to test, and it does not depend on React.

The `Field` component keeps the label, the input and the error together, so every field is accessible without extra work. You wrote the rules once in `validateSignUp`, and you can test it with plain calls.
When to show errors

items: **On submit:** the simplest. Show all errors together, and move focus to the first wrong field.
**On blur** (when the person leaves a field): friendlier for long forms. Do not show an error while the person is still typing their first attempt.
**Clear the error** as soon as the value becomes valid, so people see they fixed it.

content.text: Write messages that tell people **what to do**: “Please enter a valid email address” is better than “Invalid input”. Do not blame the person. And never rely only on colour, since some people cannot tell red from green: always include text.
Server validation always

Anything checked in the browser can be skipped by someone who sends the request directly. **The server must check everything again.** Show server errors in the same style: for example, if the server says the email is already used, put that message next to the email field.
React Hook Form: when a library helps

For large forms with many rules, a library saves time. **React Hook Form** is popular because it uses uncontrolled inputs, so the form does not redraw on every key press. You register fields and get errors from it:
npm install react-hook-form

`register('email', rules)` connects an input to the form and gives it its rules. `handleSubmit` runs your function only when all rules pass. `isSubmitting` is true while your async function runs, which is handy for disabling the button. For complex rules, you can combine it with a schema library such as Zod. Start with the plain way in this lesson, and add a library when your forms become big.
Good form habits

items: Every input has a visible `label`. A placeholder disappears when typing, so it is not a label.
Use the right `type` and `autoComplete` values (`email`, `tel`, `current-password`, `one-time-code`). Phones then show the right keyboard and can fill in details.
Disable the submit button while sending, and show progress.
Do not clear a long form when an error happens. Keep what people typed.
Keep forms short. Every extra field loses some people.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Forgetting `name` on inputs, so `FormData` is empty.
Setting the `Content-Type` header when sending `FormData`.
Checking only in the browser and not on the server.
Showing errors only in red with no text.
Using `value` without `onChange`, or mixing controlled and uncontrolled inputs in the same field.

content.text: Choosing your approach: a short guide
You now know three ways to build a form. Here is how to pick between them for a real project.

items: **Controlled inputs with state:** best when the screen must react while people type, for example a live character counter, instant formatting or a search that filters as you type.
**`FormData` with a validation function:** best for most normal forms, such as contact, sign-up and settings. Short code, no state for each field, and an easy function to test.
**React Hook Form:** best for large forms with many rules, many steps or dynamic fields, where you want less code and fewer redraws.

content.text: Whatever you choose, the same good habits apply: clear labels, helpful messages, the right input types, a disabled button while sending, and a second check on the server. A form that is easy to use is worth more than a clever one.
Questions beginners often ask
**Can I use FormData with a controlled input?** You can, but it mixes two ways. Pick one way for each form so the code stays easy to understand.
**How do I validate on blur?** Add `onBlur` to the field and run the checks for that one field, then set only that field error. Clear it when the value becomes valid.

**How do I reset a form after submit?** For an uncontrolled form, call `event.currentTarget.reset()`. For a controlled form, set the state back to the starting object. In React 19 a form action resets the form for you after it finishes.
**What is Zod?** A small library for describing the shape of data and checking it, with clear errors. You can use the same rules in the browser and on a Node server.
Your task

items: Build the sign-up form with `FormData`, `noValidate` and the `validateSignUp` function. Add a confirm password field to the rules.
Move focus to the first field with an error after a failed submit (use a ref or `querySelector`).
Show an error from a fake server response, such as “email already used”.
Rebuild the login form with React Hook Form and compare the code.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Every error appears next to its field, and disappears when fixed.
A keyboard user can reach and fix every field.
You can read the form values without any `useState` for fields.

content.text: Summary

items: `FormData` reads all fields of a form on submit. Give every input a `name`.
Use HTML validation as a first layer, and write one plain validation function for your own messages.
Show clear, helpful text errors next to fields and connect them with `aria-describedby`.
Always validate again on the server. Use React Hook Form when forms get large.

faqs.q: Should I use controlled or uncontrolled inputs?
faqs.a: Use controlled inputs when the screen must react as people type. Use FormData and uncontrolled inputs for simple or very large forms where you only need the values on submit.

faqs.q: Do I need React Hook Form?
faqs.a: Not for small forms. It helps with large forms and many rules, and it avoids a redraw on every key press.

faqs.q: Is client side validation enough?
faqs.a: No. Anyone can send a request without your form. The server must always validate the data again.

faqs.q: Why is FormData empty?
faqs.a: Inputs without a name attribute are not included. Give every input a name.

lessons.title: How React Renders: Pure Components, Re-renders, Batching and StrictMode
lessons.description: See what happens when React draws a component. Learn pure components, re-renders, batching and StrictMode.

content.text: You can build many things in React without knowing how it works inside. But when something does not behave as you expect, a clear picture of **how React draws** will save you hours. This lesson explains rendering in simple steps, and the rules that make React code predictable.
What does “render” mean?

In React, **rendering** means React **calls your component function** to find out what should be on the screen. It is not the same as drawing pixels. Rendering is only the thinking part. The function returns JSX, which is a description of the screen.
A render and the following update happens in three steps:

items: **Trigger:** something asks for a draw. This is either the first draw of the app, or a state change.
**Render:** React calls your component (and the components inside it) and gets their JSX.
**Commit:** React compares the new result with the old one, and changes **only the differences** in the real page.

content.text: If the render result is the same as last time, React changes nothing on the page, even though your function ran.
What causes a re-render?

items: A component's own **state** changes (a setter is called with a **different** value).
Its **parent** renders. By default, when a component renders, **all the components inside it render too**, even if their props did not change.
A **context** it reads changes.

content.text: That second point surprises people. React renders children by default because it is usually cheap, and because checking every component would also cost time. If a render is truly slow, you can reduce it with `memo`, which lesson 21 covers. Do not worry about it until you see a real problem.
A component re-rendering is **not** a bug. Rendering is just calling a function. The expensive part, changing the real page, only happens for real differences.
Pure components
The key rule of React: **a component must be a pure function of its props and state**. “Pure” means:

items: **Same inputs, same output.** With the same props, state and context, a component always returns the same JSX.
**No side effects while rendering.** Rendering must not change anything outside the component, such as a global variable, the page, or a server.

content.text: Compare these two:

React may call your component more than once, may pause a draw, or may throw one away and start again. This only works if rendering has no hidden effects. The place for effects is **event handlers** and **`useEffect`**, as we saw before.
Local changes are fine
A component may change things it **created itself** during the same render. For example, building a new array and filling it is fine:
What is not fine is changing the **props or state**, or things made before this render.
Immutability: never change, always replace

React finds out whether a value changed by checking if it is a **new object**. So we must not change arrays and objects in state or props. We make a new copy. This is the reason for `[...items, newItem]` and `{ ...user, name: 'x' }`.

For deep objects, copying every level by hand gets long. A small library called **Immer** (used inside Redux Toolkit and available as `useImmer`) lets you write “changes” in a safe way. Learn the plain way first.
State is a snapshot

Each render has its own copy of the state, like a photo taken at that moment. Inside a render, and inside the event handlers made during it, the values do not change, even if you call a setter. That is why this prints the old number, and why three `setCount(count + 1)` calls add only one:
The fix is the function form: `setCount((c) => c + 1)`, which works on the **latest** value instead of the snapshot.
Batching: many updates, one render

If you call several setters in one event, React waits until the handler finishes, then renders **once** with all the new values. This is called **batching**. It makes your app faster, and since React 18 it works everywhere, even inside timers and after `fetch`.
So you do not need to worry about “too many renders” when you set a few states together.
Infinite loops

If you set state **during** a render, for example `setCount(count + 1)` directly in the body of the component, React renders again, which sets state again, and so on forever. React stops it with an error: “Too many re-renders”. State must be set in event handlers or effects, not while rendering. The same happens with an effect that sets state and has no dependency array.
StrictMode: your safety net
`StrictMode` is the wrapper you saw in `main.jsx`. In development only, it:

items: Renders each component **twice** to find impure code. If your component prints something or changes a variable during render, you will see the double result.
Runs each effect, then its cleanup, then the effect again, to test that cleanup works.

content.text: This is on purpose, to help you. It does nothing in the built site, so it costs your visitors nothing. If you see something happen twice in development, check whether your code is pure and has a cleanup, instead of removing `StrictMode`.
Keys and identity

React remembers state by the **position** of a component in the tree, and by its **key**. If a component stays in the same place, it keeps its state. If it moves to a different place, or you give it a different key, React throws away the old one and makes a new one. This gives you a nice trick: to **reset** a component's state, change its key.
<ProfileForm key={userId} userId={userId} />   {/* a new form for each user */}

It also explains a bug: defining a component **inside** another component makes a brand new component type on every render, so its state is lost each time. Always define components at the top level of the file.
A simple way to debug renders

items: Add `console.log('Card render')` at the top of a component and watch how often it runs.
Use the **Profiler** tab in React Developer Tools to record a session and see what rendered and how long it took.
Ask: what triggered this? (state, parent, context). Then ask: is the work slow enough to matter? Most of the time it is not.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Changing a variable outside the component during render.
Changing state directly instead of making a new copy.
Setting state in the body of the component, which causes a loop.
Defining components inside components.
Worrying about re-renders before measuring a real problem.

content.text: Your task

items: Add a `console.log` in a parent and a child component. Click a button in the parent that changes its state, and watch which components log.
Break purity on purpose: change a global variable in a component, and see the double change in development.
Make a `Profile` form that resets when you change its `key`.
Click a button that calls `setCount(count + 1)` three times, then fix it with the function form.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can explain trigger, render and commit in your own words.
You know why a child renders when its parent renders.
The count increases by 3 after you use the function form.

content.text: Summary

items: Rendering means calling your component. React then compares results and changes only the differences in the page.
A re-render is caused by state, a parent render, or a context change. It is normal and usually cheap.
Components must be pure: same inputs give the same output, with no side effects while rendering.
Never change state or props. Make copies. State is a snapshot per render, and updates are batched.

faqs.q: Why does my component render twice in development?
faqs.a: StrictMode renders twice on purpose to help you find impure code. It does not happen in the built site.

faqs.q: Is a re-render a problem?
faqs.a: No. Re-rendering only calls your function. The page changes only where the result is different. Optimise only when you measure a real slowness.

faqs.q: Why must components be pure?
faqs.a: React may call a component more than once, or pause and restart a render. Pure components give the same result every time, so this is safe.

faqs.q: How can I reset a component state?
faqs.a: Give it a different key. React then throws away the old component and makes a new one with fresh state.
