If nothing is different, the page is left alone, even though your function ran.

lessons.title: React Performance: memo, useMemo, useCallback and When Not to Use Them
lessons.description: Find slow parts and fix them with memo, useMemo, useCallback and debounce, without adding code you do not need.

content.text: Most React apps are fast enough with no special work. But sometimes a page feels slow: typing lags, a list stutters, or a click takes a moment. This lesson explains **why** that happens and how to fix it with a few simple tools. It also explains the most important rule: **measure first, then optimise**.
Step 1: find the real problem
Do not add `memo` and `useMemo` everywhere “just in case”. They add code and need care, and often change nothing. Find the slow part first:

items: Open **React Developer Tools** and use the **Profiler** tab. Click record, do the slow action, stop, and look at which components rendered and how long each took.
Test with **CPU throttling** in the browser tools (Performance tab), because your computer is faster than many visitors' phones.
Look at the **Network** tab. Many slow pages are slow because of large images, large JavaScript files or slow requests, not because of React.

content.text: A common order of fixes, from most to least effective: send **less data and less code** first (smaller images, code splitting), then make the work **smaller** (show only what is visible), and only then **skip renders** with memo.
Why components render too much

From the last lesson: when a component renders, its children render too, even if their props did not change. Usually that is cheap. But if a child is slow (a big chart or a long list), re-rendering it every time the parent changes is wasteful. For example, typing in a text box in the parent redraws the whole big list on every key press.
Fix 1: move state down
The best and simplest fix needs no tools. Put the state in a smaller component that only contains the part that needs it:

Now typing only redraws `SearchBox`. Another version of this trick is to pass the slow part in as `children`, since children made by the parent above are not redrawn when the small component's state changes.
Fix 2: React.memo
`memo` wraps a component so React **skips rendering it when its props are the same** as last time.

React compares each prop with the old one using “is it the same value?”. For numbers and strings that is clear. For **objects, arrays and functions**, a new one is made on every render, so they are **never** the same as before, even if they look the same. That makes `memo` useless unless you keep those props steady. That is the job of the next two hooks.
Fix 3: useMemo for expensive work
`useMemo` remembers the **result** of a calculation, and recalculates only when its dependencies change.

If another state in this component changes, `visible` is not recalculated, because `products` and `query` are the same. It is useful for really heavy work, such as filtering thousands of items, and for keeping an object or array **steady** so that a `memo` child does not redraw.
Fix 4: useCallback for steady functions
`useCallback` is the same as `useMemo`, but for **functions**. It gives the same function again unless a dependency changes:

Notice we used the function form of `setItems`, so the callback does not need `items` in its dependencies, and it stays the same forever. Without `useCallback`, `handleRemove` would be a new function every render, and `memo` on `MemoRow` would do nothing.

`useMemo` and `useCallback` on their own do not make your app faster. They only help when they keep a value steady for something that **compares** it: a `memo` component, another hook's dependency list, or an expensive calculation. Using them without a reason only adds code.
The React Compiler

React now has a **compiler**, a build tool that adds this kind of memoisation automatically. When it is turned on in your project, you will need to write `useMemo`, `useCallback` and `memo` much less. It is still good to know what they do, because you will meet them in existing code. Check the official React docs to see how to enable the compiler in your tool, as the steps change.
Fix 5: show less (virtualise long lists)

If a list has thousands of rows, even fast components are slow, because the browser has to make thousands of elements. The fix is to draw only the rows you can **see**, plus a few extra. This is called **virtualisation** or windowing. Libraries such as `react-window` and TanStack Virtual do it for you. For lists of a few hundred rows, you do not need it. Pagination (showing 20 at a time) is simpler and also good for users.
Fix 6: do not do work on every key press
Searching or filtering on every key press can be heavy. Two helpers:

items: **Debounce:** wait until the person stops typing for a moment (see `useDebounce` in lesson 17).
**`useDeferredValue`:** a React hook that lets the input stay quick while the slow list catches up a little later.

content.text: The input updates at once. The list uses the slightly older `deferred` value, and React updates it when it has time, so typing never feels stuck.
Other quick wins

items: **Images:** use modern sizes and formats, set `width` and `height`, and add `loading="lazy"` for images below the fold.
**Code splitting:** load a page's code only when needed (next lesson).
**Keys:** stable keys avoid recreating list items.
**Avoid heavy work while rendering:** do not sort or parse big data in the body without `useMemo`, if it is truly big.
**Production build:** always test speed with `npm run build` and `npm run preview`. The development version is much slower on purpose.

content.text: A simple decision list

items: Is the app really slow? If not, stop.
Find the slow part with the Profiler.
Can you move state down, or pass the slow part as children? Do that first.
Is a heavy child redrawing with the same props? Add `memo`, and make object and function props steady.
Is a calculation heavy? Use `useMemo`.
Is a list very long? Paginate or virtualise.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Adding `memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` everywhere before measuring.
Wrapping a component in `memo` but passing a new object or function each time, so it never skips.
Wrong dependency arrays in `useMemo` and `useCallback`, which give old values.
Measuring speed in the development build.
Using the array index as a key in long lists that change.

content.text: Your task

items: Make a page with a text box and a list of 2,000 items. Notice the lag when typing, and fix it by moving the state down.
Wrap the list item in `memo`, add `useCallback` for a remove button, and check with the Profiler that rows no longer redraw.
Try `useDeferredValue` for a filter box.
Run the Profiler before and after each change and write down the difference.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Typing in the box does not make the whole list render in the Profiler.
Removing one item redraws only the changed parts.
You can say why `memo` needs steady props.

content.text: Summary

items: Measure first with the Profiler. Many slow pages are slow because of big images and big code, not renders.
The simplest fix is to move state down. Then use `memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` where they really help.
`memo` needs steady props. Objects and functions must be kept steady with `useMemo` and `useCallback`.
For very long lists, paginate or virtualise. Use debounce or `useDeferredValue` for typing.

faqs.q: When should I use useMemo and useCallback?
faqs.a: When a value must stay steady for a memo component or a dependency list, or when a calculation is truly heavy. Not by default.

faqs.q: Does React.memo always make my app faster?
faqs.a: No. It only helps if the component is slow and its props are the same between renders. New objects and functions as props break it.

faqs.q: Why is my app slower in development?
faqs.a: The development build adds extra checks and runs some code twice. Test speed with the production build.

faqs.q: What is virtualisation?
faqs.a: Drawing only the list rows that are visible, so very long lists stay fast. Libraries such as react-window do it.

First measure with the Profiler. Then try the simplest fix: move the state down into a small component.
If the child is still slow, wrap it in memo so React skips it when its props are the same.
Objects and functions are new on every render, so keep them steady with useMemo and useCallback.
Do not add these everywhere. Measure first, and fix only what is really slow.

lessons.title: React Code Splitting: lazy, Suspense and Faster First Load
lessons.description: Make the first load faster by loading code only when needed. Learn lazy, Suspense and route splitting.

content.text: When you build a React app, all your code is joined into files called **bundles**. The browser must download and run them before the page works. If your app is large, the first visit can be slow, especially on a phone with a weak connection. **Code splitting** means loading only the code a visitor needs now, and loading the rest later.
The idea in plain words

Think of a restaurant. You do not bring the whole kitchen to the table when someone sits down. You bring the menu first, and the food when it is ordered. In a website, the home page is the menu. The admin dashboard, the chart library and the settings page are dishes that only some visitors will order, so load them when asked.
Dynamic import

JavaScript has a feature called **dynamic `import()`**. Unlike the normal `import` at the top of a file, it loads a file **when you call it** and returns a promise. The build tool (Vite) sees this and puts that file in a separate bundle.
The PDF code is only downloaded when someone clicks the button. Visitors who never export never pay for it.
React.lazy and Suspense
React gives you `lazy` to use this idea for **components**, and `Suspense` to show something while the code is loading.

items: `lazy(() => import('./Reports.jsx'))` makes a component that loads on first use. The file must **export default** the component.
`Suspense` shows its `fallback` until the lazy component is ready. Give a helpful fallback, such as a spinner or a skeleton that has the same size as the real content, so the page does not jump.
You can put several lazy components inside one `Suspense`, and it waits for all.

content.text: The best place to split: routes
The most useful and simple place is at the **page level**. Each route becomes its own bundle, so a visitor to the home page does not download the code of the admin pages.
One `Suspense` around all the routes is enough to start. You can add smaller ones later around slow parts, so the rest of the page stays visible.
For the page a visitor lands on first, such as the home page, you may prefer **not** to make it lazy, since it is needed at once anyway. Splitting helps the other pages.
Split heavy libraries too
Big libraries, such as chart tools, rich text editors, maps and PDF makers, are often the largest part of a bundle. Load them only where they are used:
Preload: load before it is needed
A lazy page loads when the person goes there, which can feel like a small delay. You can load it a little earlier, for example when the person moves the mouse over the link:
The browser keeps the loaded file, so when the page is requested it is ready at once. This keeps the benefit of splitting without the wait.
What happens when loading fails?

A lazy file can fail to load, for example if the person goes offline, or if you deployed a new version and the old file name no longer exists. React then throws an error. You should catch it with an **error boundary**, which the next lesson covers, and show a message such as “Could not load this page. Please reload.”
Check your bundle size

Look at what `npm run build` prints. Vite shows each file and its size, and warns when a file is larger than 500 kilobytes. Many teams also use a visual tool, such as `rollup-plugin-visualizer`, which draws a map of what is in your bundle, so you can spot a single huge package.

items: Prefer smaller libraries, or import only the part you need (for example one function, not the whole utility library).
Remove packages you no longer use.
Compress images, and use modern formats.
Make sure your server sends files compressed (gzip or brotli) and with good cache headers. Files with a hash in their name can be cached for a long time.

content.text: Measure the result

Open the browser tools on the **Network** tab, turn on throttling (for example “Fast 4G”), reload the page, and look at how many kilobytes were downloaded before the page shows. Compare before and after splitting. Also test with a real phone if you can. Tools like Lighthouse in Chrome give a score and tips.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting `export default` in a file used with `lazy`.
No `Suspense` around a lazy component, which gives an error.
A fallback that is much smaller than the real content, so the page jumps when it loads.
Making tiny components lazy, which adds many small requests for no gain.
Not handling load failures.

content.text: A real example of the numbers

Here is the kind of difference splitting can make. Imagine an app with a home page, a dashboard with a chart library, and an admin area. Before splitting, the build produces one file of about 900 kilobytes. Every visitor downloads all of it, even those who never open the dashboard. After making the dashboard and admin pages lazy, the main file might drop to about 250 kilobytes, and the chart code is a separate file of 500 kilobytes that only loads for people who open the dashboard. A visitor to the home page now downloads about a quarter of what they did before.

These numbers are only an example. Your own results depend on your libraries and pages. The point is the method: build, look at the file sizes, split the biggest parts that are not needed on the first screen, and build again to compare. A few minutes of work can make the first visit much faster, especially on a phone with a slow connection.
Your task

items: Take your router app from lesson 18 and make each page lazy.
Run `npm run build` before and after. Compare the size of the main file.
Add a preload on hover for one link.
In the browser Network tab, check that a page's file loads only when you open that page.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The first load downloads less code than before.
Each page's own file appears in the Network tab only when you visit it.
The fallback appears briefly, then the page.

content.text: Summary

items: Code splitting loads code only when it is needed, so the first visit is faster.
Use `lazy(() => import('./Page.jsx'))` and wrap the result in `Suspense` with a fallback.
Split at routes first, then heavy libraries. Preload on hover to avoid delays.
Check bundle size and always handle load failures.

faqs.q: What is code splitting?
faqs.a: Dividing your app code into several files and loading each one only when the visitor needs it, so the first page loads faster.

faqs.q: Do I need Suspense with lazy?
faqs.a: Yes. Suspense shows a fallback while the lazy component loads. Without it React throws an error.

faqs.q: Where should I split my code?
faqs.a: Start with routes (one bundle per page), then split heavy libraries such as charts and editors.

faqs.q: Why does the page jump when a lazy component loads?
faqs.a: The fallback is smaller than the real content. Make the fallback about the same size, for example a skeleton.

lessons.title: React Error Boundaries and Portals: Safe Crashes, Modals and Tooltips
lessons.description: Stop one bug from crashing the whole page with error boundaries, and build safe modals and tooltips with portals.

content.text: Things go wrong in real apps: a server sends strange data, a component has a bug, a lazy file fails to load. Without a plan, one small error can turn the **whole page white**. In this lesson you will learn **error boundaries**, which keep the rest of the page working, and **portals**, which let a component draw somewhere else in the page, for example for a modal.
What happens when a component throws

If an error happens while React is rendering a component (for example `user.name` when `user` is `null`), React removes the whole component tree from the screen. The visitor sees a blank page. That is much worse than a small message in one box.
An **error boundary** is a component that catches such errors in the components below it, and shows a **fallback** instead. The rest of the page keeps working.
Writing an error boundary
Error boundaries are the one thing in React that still must be a **class component**, because there is no hook for it yet. You write it once and use it everywhere:

items: `getDerivedStateFromError` runs when a child throws, and sets `hasError` to true, so the next render shows the fallback.
`componentDidCatch` is where you **report** the error, to the console or to a monitoring service.
`render` shows the fallback when there is an error, and the normal children otherwise.

content.text: You can also use the ready-made package `react-error-boundary`, which gives you the same with a function-friendly API and a handy reset button. Many teams use it.
Using it

If `SalesChart` crashes, only that box shows the message. The header and the comments stay. This is the idea: **put boundaries around parts that can fail independently**. A good plan is one boundary around the whole app as a last safety net, and smaller ones around risky parts such as widgets, charts and lazy pages.
What error boundaries do not catch

items: **Errors in event handlers** (a click handler that throws). Use a normal `try` and `catch` there.
**Errors in async code**, such as inside `fetch` promises or `setTimeout`. Catch them yourself and put the error in state, as in the fetching lesson.
**Server rendering errors**, and errors in the boundary itself.

content.text: A retry button
A fallback is more useful with a way to try again. Use a `key` to reset the boundary and its children:
When `attempt` changes, the `key` changes, so React makes a brand new boundary with no error. The chart tries to load again.
Portals: draw somewhere else

A modal (a box that appears above the page) is a problem if it sits deep in your component tree. A parent with `overflow: hidden` or a `z-index` can cut it off or hide it. A **portal** lets a component render its output in a **different place in the real page**, such as directly under `<body>`, while still being part of the same React tree. That means props, state and context still work normally.

`createPortal(jsx, container)` draws the JSX inside `container`, here `document.body`. The click on the dark backdrop closes the modal, and `stopPropagation` makes sure that clicking inside the box does not.
Making a modal accessible
A modal that looks fine can still be hard to use. These points matter for people who use keyboards and screen readers:

items: Give the box `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"` and a name through `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.
**Move focus** into the modal when it opens, and **return focus** to the button that opened it when it closes.
Close with the **Escape** key.
**Trap the focus** inside while it is open, so Tab does not move to the page behind.
Stop the page behind from scrolling while the modal is open.

content.text: Getting all of these right by hand is work. The built-in HTML `<dialog>` element does a lot of it for you (focus handling, Escape and a backdrop) when opened with `showModal()`, and libraries like Radix UI or React Aria give tested, accessible modals. For production apps, using one of them is often the wisest choice.
Other good uses of portals

items: **Tooltips and dropdown menus** that must not be clipped by a parent.
**Toast messages** (small notices at a corner of the screen).
**Full-screen loading overlays.**

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Having no error boundary, so one bug makes the whole page white.
Expecting a boundary to catch errors in click handlers or in `fetch`. Use `try` and `catch`.
A fallback with no way to retry or leave.
A modal without Escape, focus handling and a role.
Using a modal when a simple inline message would be kinder.

content.text: Where to put error boundaries
A common question is how many boundaries an app needs. A good plan has three layers.

items: **One around the whole app.** This is the last safety net. If everything else fails, the visitor sees a friendly page with a reload button, not a white screen.
**One around each page or route.** If one page crashes, the menu and the layout stay, and the visitor can go to another page.
**Small ones around risky widgets,** such as a chart, a map, a comments box or any part that depends on data you do not control.

content.text: Always **report** what the boundary catches. A boundary that hides errors but never tells you about them means you will not know that visitors are having problems. Send the error to a logging service, or at least to your server logs. Then fix the cause, not just the message.
Your task

items: Add the `ErrorBoundary` to your app and create a component that throws on a button click state to test it.
Add a retry button using `key`.
Build a `Modal` with a portal, an Escape key close and a backdrop click close.
Move focus into the modal on open, and back to the button on close.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A crash in one widget leaves the rest of the page working.
Pressing Escape closes the modal.
After the modal closes, focus returns to the button that opened it.

content.text: Summary

items: An error boundary catches errors from components below it and shows a fallback instead of a white page.
It does not catch errors in event handlers or async code, so use `try` and `catch` there.
A portal draws a component into another place in the page, such as `document.body`, and is ideal for modals and tooltips.
Make modals accessible with a role, focus handling and Escape, or use a tested library.

faqs.q: What is an error boundary?
faqs.a: A component that catches errors from the components below it while rendering, and shows a fallback instead of crashing the whole page.

faqs.q: Why is there no hook for error boundaries?
faqs.a: React does not yet have a hook for it, so an error boundary is written as a class. The react-error-boundary package gives an easy version.

faqs.q: What is a React portal?
faqs.a: A way to draw a component into a different part of the real page, such as document.body, while it stays part of the same React tree.

faqs.q: Why does my modal get cut off?

lessons.title: React State Management: Redux Toolkit and Zustand Explained for Beginners
lessons.description: Learn when you need a state library. See the same cart built with Redux Toolkit and with Zustand.

content.text: So far we kept state with `useState`, `useReducer` and context. For many apps that is enough. But as an app grows, you may want one **central store** that any component can read and change, with good tools. In this lesson we look at the two most popular choices: **Redux Toolkit** and **Zustand**.
Do you need a state library?
Most beginners reach for a library too early. First, ask what kind of state you have:

items: **Local UI state** (a toggle, a text box): use `useState`. Keep it local.
**Server data** (lists from an API): use a data library like TanStack Query (next lesson). This is the biggest source of state in many apps, and a state library is *not* the best tool for it.
**Shared client state** (the cart, the signed-in user, filters used on many pages): this is where a store helps.

content.text: A library may be worth adding when many components far apart change the same data, when the update rules are complex, or when you want good debugging tools. If a few contexts do the job, keep them.
Redux in one picture

Redux keeps all shared state in **one store**. Components do not change it directly. They **dispatch actions**, and **reducers** (pure functions) make the new state, the same idea you learned in the `useReducer` lesson. Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the modern, official way to write Redux. It removes most of the old boilerplate.
npm install @reduxjs/toolkit react-redux
A cart with Redux Toolkit
Step 1: make a **slice**, which holds the state, the reducers and the actions of one feature together:

Look: inside the reducers it seems we **change** the state with `push` and `+= 1`. That is allowed here, because RTK uses a library called Immer behind the scenes. Immer lets you write simple “changes”, and it turns them into safe, new copies for you. This works **only** inside `createSlice` reducers.
Step 2: make the store and give it to the app:
Step 3: read and change the store in components, with `useSelector` and `useDispatch`:

items: `useSelector(fn)` picks the part of the state you need. The component redraws only when **that picked value** changes.
`useDispatch()` gives the `dispatch` function. `added(product)` makes the action `{ type: 'cart/added', payload: product }`.
Select the **smallest** piece you need, not the whole state, so fewer components redraw.

content.text: Redux also has excellent developer tools (the Redux DevTools browser extension), where you can see every action, and go back in time. For big teams and complex apps this is very valuable.
The same cart with Zustand
**Zustand** is a very small library with almost no setup. There is no provider and no actions to write. You make a **store as a hook**:
npm install zustand

The store is a hook. Components pick what they need with a selector, and call the functions in the store directly. With Zustand you still update state the immutable way (a new array or object), unless you add its `immer` helper. There is no provider, so the setup is tiny.
Redux Toolkit or Zustand?

items: **Zustand:** small, easy, fast to learn. A great choice for small and medium apps, and for a few shared values.
**Redux Toolkit:** more structure, great devtools, and a large community and ecosystem. A good fit for large apps and big teams that value strict patterns.
**Context + useReducer:** zero extra libraries, fine when state is small and changes rarely.

content.text: Neither is “better”. If you are unsure, start with the simplest one that works, because it is easy to move to a bigger tool later. The ideas you learned (actions, reducers, selectors, immutability) are the same.
Rules that work with any store

items: **Keep local state local.** Do not put a text box value in the global store.
**Keep server data in a data library**, not in your store (see lesson 25).
**Store the minimum**, and calculate the rest with selectors.
**Select small pieces** to avoid extra renders.
**Never put non-serialisable things** (functions, class instances) in a Redux store.

content.text: Saving the store

To keep the cart after a reload, save it in `localStorage`. Zustand has a `persist` helper for this. In Redux you subscribe to the store or use a library such as `redux-persist`. Do not save sensitive data in `localStorage`.
Common mistakes

items: Adding a library before you need it.
Putting every little value in the global store.
Selecting the whole state in `useSelector`, which redraws the component on any change.
Changing the state outside `createSlice` reducers in Redux, which breaks the rules.
Storing API data in the store and writing loading and error code by hand.

content.text: A decision in three questions
When you start a new feature and wonder whether you need a store, ask these questions in order.

items: **Is it data from a server?** Use a data library. Do not copy it into a store.
**Does only one component, or one parent and child, use it?** Use local state or props.
**Do many far-apart components change it, and do the rules take real effort?** Now a store such as Zustand or Redux Toolkit is a good fit.

content.text: Notice that most data fails the first two tests. That is normal. A well-built app often has very little global client state: maybe the user, a cart, and a few settings. Keeping the store small makes the app easier to understand, and easier to move to a different tool if you ever need to.
Questions beginners often ask

**Can I use Redux and TanStack Query together?** Yes, and it is a common setup. TanStack Query handles server data, and Redux Toolkit or Zustand holds shared client state such as filters and the cart.
**Will a store make my app faster?** Not by itself. A store changes where state lives. It can reduce extra renders when you select small pieces, but it is not a speed tool.
**Is Redux hard to learn?** Redux Toolkit is much easier than the old Redux. If you understood `useReducer` in lesson 15, you already know the main idea of actions and reducers.
**Do I need to wrap Zustand in a provider?** No. A Zustand store is a hook you can import and use anywhere, which is part of why it is quick to start with.
Your task

items: Build the cart with Redux Toolkit: slice, store, provider, `useSelector`, `useDispatch`.
Build the same cart with Zustand. Compare how many files and lines each needed.
Show the total price using a selector.
Install the Redux DevTools extension and watch the actions as you click Add.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The cart count is the same in the header and the cart page, in both versions.
In the Redux DevTools you can see each action.
Only components that use changed data redraw.

content.text: Summary

items: Use a state library only for shared client state that is complex. Keep local state local, and use a data library for server data.
Redux Toolkit: slices, `configureStore`, `useSelector` and `useDispatch`. Immer lets you write simple updates inside slices.
Zustand: a store as a hook with `create`, no provider, tiny setup.
Select small pieces of state, store the minimum, and keep actions clear.

faqs.q: Do I need Redux in 2026?
faqs.a: Not for most small apps. Local state, context and a data library cover many cases. Redux Toolkit is still a good choice for large apps that need structure and strong tools.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Redux and Zustand?
faqs.a: Zustand is smaller and simpler, with no provider and few concepts. Redux Toolkit has more structure, tools and conventions, which help large teams.

faqs.q: Why can I change state inside createSlice?
faqs.a: Redux Toolkit uses Immer, which turns your simple changes into safe immutable updates. It works only inside createSlice reducers.

faqs.q: Should API data go in the store?
faqs.a: Usually no. A data library such as TanStack Query handles caching, loading and refreshing for you.

lessons.title: TanStack Query (React Query): Fetching, Caching and Updating Server Data
lessons.description: Load, cache and update server data with TanStack Query. Learn useQuery, query keys, mutations and refetching.

content.text: In lesson 12 you wrote data loading by hand: loading state, error state, cancelling old requests. It works, but you repeat it in every component, and many things are still missing: caching, refreshing, retrying, and keeping the screen in step after a change. **TanStack Query**, also called **React Query**, solves all of this. It is one of the most useful libraries in the React world.
Server state is different

Data that comes from a server is not like your own UI state. It lives somewhere else, it can change without you knowing, it can be shared by many components, and it can become **stale** (out of date). Handling that with `useState` and `useEffect` is hard to do well. TanStack Query is built for exactly this kind of state, so you can stop writing that code.
Install and set up
npm install @tanstack/react-query
The `QueryClient` is the cache. The provider makes it available to every component, like the context you saw before.
useQuery: reading data
Compare this with lesson 12: there is no `useEffect`, no three `useState` calls, and no `AbortController`. You give two things:

items: **`queryKey`**: an array that **names** this data. It works like an address in the cache.
**`queryFn`**: a function that returns a promise with the data. If it throws, the query is in the error state.

content.text: You get back flags such as `isPending`, `isError`, `data` and `error`, and a `refetch` function. Note that `fetch` does not throw on a 404, so we check `response.ok` and throw ourselves.
Query keys: the heart of caching
The key identifies the data. Two components that ask for the same key share **one** request and **one** cached result. If the key has a variable in it, a new value means a new query:

When `id` changes from 1 to 2, the key changes from `['post', 1]` to `['post', 2]`, so TanStack Query loads post 2. If you go back to post 1, it shows the **cached** result at once and refreshes it quietly in the background. That is why apps built with it feel fast. Race conditions, where old data overwrites new data, are handled for you.
Stale data and refetching

Cached data is marked **stale** after a time, and by default that time is zero, so data refetches in the background when a component mounts, when the window gets focus again, and when the connection comes back. You can change this with `staleTime`, how long the data counts as fresh:

For data that rarely changes, use a long `staleTime`. For live data such as prices, use a short one, or add `refetchInterval`. Failed requests are also **retried** a few times by default, which is kind to flaky connections.
useMutation: changing data
Reading uses `useQuery`. **Creating, updating and deleting** use `useMutation`:

items: `mutate(data)` runs the `mutationFn`.
`isPending`, `isError` and `isSuccess` tell you the state, so you can disable the button and show messages.
`onSuccess` runs when it works. Here we call **`invalidateQueries`**, which marks every query with the key `['posts']` as stale, so the list **reloads by itself** and shows the new post.

content.text: This is a very nice pattern: after any change, you invalidate the related keys, and the screen stays correct without you wiring state by hand.
Optimistic updates (a short look)

Sometimes you want the screen to change **at once**, before the server answers, for example when ticking a to-do item. This is an **optimistic update**. You update the cache straight away, and if the server fails, you put the old data back. TanStack Query supports this with `onMutate` and `onError`, and there is a guide in its documentation. Use it for actions that almost always succeed. It is a small thing that makes an app feel very fast.
Where to put your queries
Do not write fetch code inside every component. Put your query functions in one file (such as `api.js`), and wrap a query in a **custom hook**, as in lesson 17:
Now every component that needs posts shares one cache entry and one request, and changing how posts are fetched happens in one place.
Developer tools
TanStack Query has a devtools panel (`@tanstack/react-query-devtools`) that shows every query, whether it is fresh or stale, and its cached data. It is a great way to learn what the library is doing.
When not to use it

items: For a tiny app with one simple request, plain `fetch` in an effect is fine.
For data that never comes from a server, use normal state.
If you use a framework such as Next.js, it has its own data tools, which you can still combine with TanStack Query.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to throw on non-OK responses in `queryFn`, so errors look like success.
Putting a changing value in `queryFn` but not in `queryKey`, so the cache shows the wrong data. **Everything the query depends on belongs in the key.**
Copying query data into `useState`. Use `data` directly.
Not invalidating after a mutation, so the list stays old.
Forgetting the `QueryClientProvider`.

content.text: Before and after: the same screen

Look at what you wrote in lesson 12 for a simple list: three pieces of state, an effect, a try and catch block, a finally block, and an abort controller. That was about thirty lines, and it still did not cache, retry or refresh. With `useQuery` the same screen is a few lines, and it gains all of those features. This is the reason the library is so popular: it removes code you would write over and over, and does it better than most hand-written versions.

It is still worth understanding the manual way first, as you did in lesson 12. When you know what loading, error and race conditions are, the library makes sense, and you can find the cause when something goes wrong. Learn the problem first, then the tool that solves it.
Your task

items: Install the library and rewrite the posts list from lesson 12 with `useQuery`. Compare the number of lines.
Add a page for one post using `['post', id]`. Go back and forth and notice the instant cached result.
Add a form with `useMutation` that creates a post and invalidates the list.
Add the devtools and watch queries become stale.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The list shows Loading, then the data, and an error with a retry button when the URL is wrong.
Going back to a visited page shows data at once.
A new item appears in the list after saving, with no manual refresh.

content.text: Summary

items: TanStack Query manages server state: caching, refetching, retries and cancelling are built in.
`useQuery({ queryKey, queryFn })` reads data. The key names the data, and everything the query depends on goes in it.
`useMutation` changes data, and `invalidateQueries` refreshes the related lists.
Wrap queries in custom hooks and keep them in one place.

faqs.q: What is TanStack Query used for?
faqs.a: For loading and changing data from a server, with caching, refetching, retries and loading and error states built in.

faqs.q: Is React Query the same as TanStack Query?
faqs.a: Yes. React Query was renamed TanStack Query when it grew to support other frameworks. The React package is @tanstack/react-query.

faqs.q: What is a query key?
faqs.a: An array that names a piece of data in the cache. Queries with the same key share one request and one result. Put every variable the query depends on in it.

faqs.q: Do I still need Redux if I use TanStack Query?
faqs.a: Often not for server data. You may still use a small store for shared client state.

lessons.title: Testing React Apps with Vitest and React Testing Library
lessons.description: Write tests that act like a user with Vitest and React Testing Library. Test forms, data loading and hooks.

content.text: A test is a small program that checks that your code still works. When you change something next month, tests tell you at once if you broke something else. Many beginners skip tests because they feel like extra work. In this lesson you will see that a few good tests are quick to write, and that they make changing code much less scary.
What should you test?
Do not try to test everything. Test what **matters to the user**, and what is easy to break:

items: **Plain functions** with rules, such as validation or price calculations. These are the easiest and most valuable tests.
**Components** the way a person uses them: the person sees text, clicks buttons and types in fields.
**Important flows**: sign in, add to cart, submit a form, an error message after a failed request.

content.text: A good guide from the testing library's own creators: **test what the user sees and does, not how your code is built inside**. If you test internal details like state names, your tests break when you tidy your code, even though the app still works. Those are bad tests.
The tools

items: **Vitest** is the test runner. It works with Vite, so it needs almost no setup, and it is very fast. (Jest is an older, similar tool you may see in other projects.)
**React Testing Library** draws your component in a fake browser and gives you ways to find things the way a user would: by text, by label and by role.
**jest-dom** adds helpful checks like “is this in the page?”.
**user-event** pretends to be a real person clicking and typing.

content.text: npm install -D vitest jsdom @testing-library/react @testing-library/jest-dom @testing-library/user-event
Then add this to `vite.config.js`, and a setup file:
`npm test` starts Vitest in watch mode: it reruns the tests you changed as you save. `npm run test:run` runs once, which is what you use in a build.
Your first test: a plain function

items: `describe` groups tests. `it` (or `test`) is one test with a clear sentence about what should happen.
`expect(value).toBe(expected)` is an **assertion**. If it is not true, the test fails and shows you the difference.

content.text: Testing a component

The test follows what a person does: draw the component, see “Count: 0”, click the button named “Add one”, see “Count: 1”. It says nothing about `useState`. If you later rewrite the counter with `useReducer`, this test still passes, which is exactly the point.
Finding things: the query priority
Testing Library suggests finding elements the way people and assistive tools do. Use them in this order:

items: `getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })`: the best. It also checks that your page is accessible.
`getByLabelText('Email')`: for form fields.
`getByText('Welcome')`: for text content.
`getByPlaceholderText`, `getByAltText`, `getByTitle`: when the above do not fit.
`getByTestId('x')`: last resort, using a `data-testid` attribute.

content.text: There are three families: **`getBy`** throws if the thing is missing, **`queryBy`** returns `null` (use it to check that something is **not** there), and **`findBy`** waits for it to appear (use it for async changes).
Testing a form

`vi.fn()` makes a **mock function**: a fake function that remembers how it was called. We pass it in as `onSubmit` and check that it was (or was not) called. Notice also that finding fields **by label** forces your form to have proper labels.
Testing async data
For components that load data, do not call the real server in a test. It would be slow and unreliable. Replace `fetch` with a fake:

`findByText` waits (for up to a second by default) until the text appears. Testing both the happy path and the error path is important, because errors are where real apps break. For bigger projects, a tool called **MSW** (Mock Service Worker) fakes the network at a deeper level, so you do not need to stub `fetch` in every test.
Testing a custom hook

`renderHook` runs your hook inside a tiny test component. `act` makes sure React has finished updating before you check the result. Testing Library's own helpers like `user.click` already wrap `act` for you.
Testing with context and a router
A component that uses context or React Router needs the provider around it. Make a small helper:
`MemoryRouter` is a router that keeps the address in memory, so no real browser is needed.
What makes a good test

items: It has a **clear name** that reads like a sentence: “shows an error for a short password”.
It tests **one idea**.
It does **not depend on other tests** or on the order they run.
It uses **no real network, timers or dates** when it can fake them.
It would **still pass** if you rewrote the inside of the component but kept the behaviour.

content.text: Do not chase 100 percent coverage. A few tests on your most important paths are worth more than many tests on trivial things. When you fix a bug, **write a test that fails because of the bug first**. Then fix it. The bug can never silently return.
Beyond component tests

items: **End-to-end tests** with Playwright or Cypress open a real browser and click through your whole app, including the server. They are slower, so write a few for the most important journeys, such as sign up and checkout.
**Continuous integration (CI)** runs your tests automatically on every push, for example with GitHub Actions, so a broken change is caught before it goes live.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Testing internal state or function names instead of what the user sees.
Using `getByTestId` for everything, which skips accessibility checks.
Forgetting `await` with `user.click` and `findBy`, so the test checks too early.
Calling real APIs in tests.
Tests that depend on each other, or on the current date.

content.text: Your task

items: Install Vitest and Testing Library, and write two tests for a `totalPrice` function.
Write a test for a counter: click, and check the new text.
Write a test for your sign-up form: a short password shows an error, and a good one calls `onSubmit`.
Write a test for a component that loads data, with a fake `fetch`, for both success and failure.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `npm run test:run` passes and prints a list of your tests.
Changing the inside of a component (for example from `useState` to `useReducer`) does not break its test.
You can break a feature on purpose and see a test fail.

content.text: Summary

items: Test what users see and do. Start with plain functions, then the key components and flows.
Use Vitest to run tests, React Testing Library to draw components, and user-event to click and type.
Find elements by role, label and text. Use `findBy` for async changes and `queryBy` to check something is absent.
Fake the network. Test both success and error paths. Run tests in CI.

faqs.q: Should I use Jest or Vitest?
faqs.a: Vitest works with Vite and needs little setup. Jest is older and also common. The API is very similar, so skills carry over.

faqs.q: What is React Testing Library?
faqs.a: A library that draws components in a test environment and finds elements the way a user would, by role, label and text.

faqs.q: How many tests should I write?
faqs.a: Enough to protect your important flows and rules. Chasing 100 percent coverage wastes time. When you fix a bug, add a test for it.

faqs.q: Why is my async test failing?
faqs.a: You probably forgot await, or used getBy instead of findBy for something that appears later.

lessons.title: React Accessibility (a11y): Build Apps Everyone Can Use
lessons.description: Build apps everyone can use: real HTML, labels, keyboard use, focus, colour contrast and how to test it.

content.text: Accessibility, often written **a11y**, means making your app usable by **everyone**, including people who are blind, have low vision, cannot use a mouse, are deaf, or have trouble reading or focusing. It also helps people on a bright street, with one hand free, or with a slow connection. In many countries it is also a legal requirement for some kinds of sites. The good news: most of it is simple, and React makes it as easy as plain HTML.
Who benefits?

items: **Screen reader users** hear the page read aloud. They depend on correct structure and labels.
**Keyboard users** move with Tab, Enter, Space and the arrow keys, with no mouse.
**People with low vision** zoom the page, use large text, or need high colour contrast.
**People with colour blindness** cannot rely on colour alone.
**People with hearing loss** need captions for video and audio.
**People with attention or reading difficulties** benefit from clear, simple, predictable pages.

content.text: Rule 1: use the right HTML element

This is the most powerful rule. Browsers and screen readers already understand real HTML elements. A real `button` can be reached with Tab, pressed with Enter and Space, and is announced as a button, all for free. A `div` with an `onClick` has none of that.

items: Use `button` for actions and `a` (or `Link`) for navigation.
Use headings `h1` to `h6` in order, with one `h1` per page. They are the outline of your page.
Use `nav`, `main`, `header`, `footer`, `section` and `article` for the page layout.
Use `ul` and `li` for lists, and `table` with `th` for real tables of data.

content.text: These elements are called **semantic HTML**. Using them gives you most of accessibility with no extra code.
Rule 2: label everything

items: Every form field needs a visible `label`, connected with `htmlFor` and `id`. A placeholder is not a label.
Every meaningful image needs `alt` text that says what it **means**. A decorative image gets an empty `alt=""` so screen readers skip it.
Buttons that show only an icon need a name: `<button aria-label="Close">X</button>`.
Links should make sense alone. “Read our pricing guide” is better than “click here”.

content.text: In React, you can make unique ids with the `useId` hook, which is safe to use when a component appears many times on one page:
Rule 3: the keyboard must work

Put your mouse away and try your app with only the keyboard. Can you reach everything with Tab? Can you see where you are? Can you press every button with Enter or Space? Can you leave a modal with Escape?

items: Keep the **focus outline** visible. Never write `outline: none` without giving a clear replacement, such as a coloured ring with `:focus-visible`.
The **Tab order** should follow the visual order. Avoid positive `tabIndex` values. Use `tabIndex={0}` only for rare custom controls, and `tabIndex={-1}` to allow focusing an element from code.
Add a **skip link** at the top of the page that jumps to the main content, so keyboard users do not Tab through the whole menu on every page.
Never trap focus, except inside an open modal, where it must stay until the modal closes.

content.text:
Skip to main content ...
...
Rule 4: do not rely on colour alone

items: Text needs enough **contrast** with its background. The common guide is at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text, and 3 to 1 for large text. Browser tools can check this for you.
Do not show an error only with red. Add an icon or text such as “Error: ...”.
Links inside text should be underlined or otherwise clearly different, not only a different colour.
Respect **reduced motion**: some people feel sick from animation. Use `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` to turn it off.

content.text: ARIA: use it when HTML is not enough

**ARIA** attributes add extra information for assistive technology. The first rule of ARIA is: **do not use ARIA if a normal HTML element can do the job**. Wrong ARIA is worse than none. When you really need it, these are the most common attributes:

items: `aria-label`: gives a name to an element that has no visible text.
`aria-labelledby`: names an element using another element's text.
`aria-describedby`: connects help or error text to a field.
`aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`: tell if a menu or panel is open, and what it controls.
`aria-live="polite"` or `role="status"`: announces changes, such as “Item added to cart”.
`role="alert"`: announces an important message at once, such as an error.
`aria-hidden="true"`: hides decoration from screen readers.

content.text: Announce changes
When something changes on the page without a reload (a message, a count, a loaded list), a screen reader user may not notice. A **live region** announces it:

Keep announcements short, and do not announce every tiny change.
Single page apps: route changes
In a normal website, loading a new page tells the screen reader that something changed. In a React app with a router, the page changes silently. Help the user by moving focus and updating the title:
Also give every page a unique, helpful `document.title`.
Test accessibility

items: **Use only the keyboard** for a few minutes. It reveals most problems.
**ESLint plugin `jsx-a11y`** warns about problems as you type (it is included in many React starters).
**Lighthouse** (in Chrome) and the **axe DevTools** extension scan a page for common problems.
**Turn on a screen reader**: VoiceOver on Mac and iPhone, TalkBack on Android, NVDA (free) on Windows. Even a short try is eye-opening.
**React Testing Library** queries like `getByRole` and `getByLabelText` fail when your markup is not accessible.

content.text: Automated tools find only part of the problems, often said to be less than half. They are a good start, but they cannot tell if your `alt` text is helpful or if the page makes sense. Always add a manual check.
A quick checklist

items: Real `button`, `a`, `nav`, `main`, and heading elements in the right order.
Every field has a label, every image has suitable `alt`.
Everything works with the keyboard and the focus is always visible.
Text contrast is good, and colour is never the only signal.
Errors and changes are announced, and route changes are handled.
Animation can be reduced, and text can be zoomed to 200 percent without breaking.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Using `div` for buttons and links.
Removing the focus outline.
Using placeholder text as the only label.
Adding ARIA that does not match what the element really does.
Skipping heading levels or using headings only for size.
Forgetting that route changes are silent.

content.text: Your task

items: Unplug your mouse and use your app with only the keyboard. Write down every problem.
Fix one: replace a `div` button with a real button, and add a visible focus style.
Add a skip link and make sure every form field has a label.
Run Lighthouse and fix the first three accessibility issues it reports.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can reach and use every control with only the keyboard.
A screen reader reads each field with its label.
Lighthouse shows a high accessibility score and no contrast errors.

content.text: Summary

items: Use semantic HTML first: real buttons, links, headings and landmarks.
Label fields, add `alt` text, keep focus visible, and make everything work with a keyboard.
Do not rely on colour alone, and keep good contrast.
Use ARIA only when needed, announce changes, handle route changes, and test with a keyboard, tools and a screen reader.

faqs.q: What is accessibility in web development?
faqs.a: Building websites and apps that people with disabilities, and everyone else, can use, including with keyboards, screen readers and zoom.

faqs.q: Do I need ARIA for everything?
faqs.a: No. Use semantic HTML first. Add ARIA only when HTML cannot do the job. Wrong ARIA can make things worse.

faqs.q: How do I test accessibility in React?
faqs.a: Use the keyboard only, run Lighthouse or axe, use the jsx-a11y ESLint plugin, and try a screen reader. Automated tools find only part of the problems.

faqs.q: What is the minimum colour contrast?
faqs.a: A common guide is 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text. Browser developer tools can show the ratio.

lessons.title: React 19 New Features: Actions, useActionState, useOptimistic, use and More
lessons.description: The main React 19 tools in simple words: form actions, useActionState, useOptimistic, use and ref as a prop.

content.text: React 19 added several features that make common jobs, such as forms and data loading, shorter and easier. You do not need them to build good apps, and older code that uses the earlier ways keeps working. But you will see these tools in new projects, so it is good to know what they do. This lesson explains each one with a small example.
React moves fast, and details can change between versions. This lesson covers the main ideas of React 19. For exact and current details, check the official React documentation at react.dev.
The big idea: Actions

An **action** is a function that does something with data, usually asynchronous, such as sending a form to a server. React 19 lets you pass a function to a form's `action` prop. React runs it for you when the form is submitted, handles the “pending” period, and resets the form fields after a good submit.

Compare this with the forms in lessons 9 and 19: there is no `onSubmit`, no `preventDefault`, no `FormData` call, and no state for the fields. React gives your function the `FormData` for you. The form also works as a plain HTML form if JavaScript is slow to load.
useActionState: results, errors and pending
An action usually needs to give something back, like an error message or a success note. `useActionState` connects an action to state:

items: The action receives the **previous state** as its first argument, and the `FormData` as the second.
Whatever the action **returns** becomes the new `state`.
`useActionState` gives you `[state, formAction, isPending]`. Use `formAction` in the form, and `isPending` to disable the button.

content.text: Forms that need validation, errors and a loading state become much shorter. Remember, as always, to **validate again on the server**.
useFormStatus: a button that knows
A submit button deep in a component tree can know whether its parent form is sending, without any props, using `useFormStatus` from `react-dom`:
It must be used in a component that is **inside** the form, not in the component that renders the form itself.
useOptimistic: update at once, fix later

When someone clicks a heart or sends a chat message, waiting for the server makes the page feel slow. An **optimistic update** shows the expected result **immediately**, and returns to the real state if the request fails. `useOptimistic` makes this easy:

The optimistic value is used **only while the action runs**. When it finishes, React uses the real `messages` again. If the request failed, the temporary message simply disappears, since the real state never included it. Show an error message to explain.
The use API

`use` is a new function that reads a value that may not be ready yet. It can read a **promise**, and it can read **context**. When given a promise, it pauses the component until the promise is done, and shows the nearest `Suspense` fallback meanwhile.

An important point: the promise should be created **outside** the rendering component, for example by a parent, a router loader, a framework or a data library, and passed down. If you create a new promise inside the component that calls `use`, it will create a new one every render and loop. For most apps, a library such as TanStack Query or a framework handles this for you. Unlike other hooks, `use` can be called inside an `if` or a loop. When reading context, `use(MyContext)` works like `useContext`.
ref as a normal prop
Before React 19, passing a ref through your own component needed `forwardRef`. Now `ref` is simply a prop that function components can receive:
Refs can also have a **cleanup function** now: a ref callback may return a function that React calls when the element is removed.
Document metadata in components
You can now write `title`, `meta` and `link` tags **anywhere in your components**, and React moves them into the `head` of the page for you:

This replaces the need for a helper library for simple cases. Remember that a page drawn only in the browser is harder for search engines to read, so for pages that must rank well, think about server rendering.
Smaller improvements

items: **Context as a provider:** you can write `<ThemeContext value="dark">` instead of `<ThemeContext.Provider value="dark">`.
**Better error reporting:** clearer messages, and options to report errors caught and not caught.
**Support for custom elements** (web components).
**Stylesheets and scripts:** better control of loading order and avoiding duplicates.
**Preloading helpers** such as `preload` and `preconnect` in `react-dom`.

content.text: The React Compiler and Server Components

Two bigger ideas go with this release. The **React Compiler** is a build tool that adds memoisation for you, so you write less `useMemo` and `useCallback`. **Server Components** let some components run only on the server and send results to the browser, which is used by frameworks such as Next.js. You do not need either to start. Learn them after you are comfortable with everything in this course.
Should you use these features now?

items: If you start a new project on React 19, yes: form actions and `useActionState` make forms shorter.
If your project uses an older version, the old ways (`onSubmit`, `useState`) still work, and you can upgrade later.
Keep using a data library for server data. `use` is a building block, not a replacement for caching.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Calling `useFormStatus` in the same component that renders the form. It must be in a child.
Creating the promise inside the component that calls `use`.
Forgetting `name` on inputs, so the `FormData` has no values.
Trusting only the client check. Always validate on the server.
Using optimistic updates for actions that often fail.

content.text: Your task

items: Make a newsletter form with a form action and no `onSubmit`.
Rewrite your sign-up form with `useActionState` and show the pending state and error.
Add a `SubmitButton` that uses `useFormStatus`.
Add an optimistic message list that shows new messages at once.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The form works with no `preventDefault` code.
The button is disabled and shows “Creating...” while the request runs.
A new message appears immediately, and disappears if you make the fake request fail.

content.text: Summary

items: Form `action` takes a function that receives the `FormData`. `useActionState` adds result, error and pending state.
`useFormStatus` lets a child button know that its form is sending. `useOptimistic` shows expected results at once.
`use` reads a promise or context, and works with `Suspense`. `ref` is now a normal prop.
You can render `title` and `meta` tags in components. The old ways still work.

faqs.q: What is new in React 19?
faqs.a: Form actions, useActionState, useFormStatus, useOptimistic, the use API, ref as a prop, document metadata in components, and other smaller improvements.

faqs.q: Do I have to upgrade to React 19?
faqs.a: No. Older ways keep working. Upgrade when you are ready, or start new projects on the latest version.

faqs.q: What is useOptimistic?
faqs.a: A hook that shows an expected result immediately while a request is running, and goes back to the real state if the request fails.

faqs.q: Is use the same as useEffect for fetching?
faqs.a: No. use reads a promise that was created outside the component and waits with Suspense. Data libraries or frameworks usually create and cache those promises.

steps.say: You pass a function to the form action. React gives it the FormData.
useActionState keeps the result, an error message and the pending flag for you.
useOptimistic shows the expected result on screen right away.
Meanwhile the real request goes to the server.
If it works, the real data replaces the guess. If it fails, the guess disappears and you show an error.

lessons.title: React with TypeScript: A Beginner Guide to Typing Props, State and Events
lessons.description: Learn TypeScript for React: type props, state, events, refs and API data, and understand the errors it shows.

content.text: **TypeScript** is JavaScript with **types**. A type says what kind of value something is: a number, a piece of text, a list of users. TypeScript checks this while you write, and underlines mistakes in your editor **before** you run the app. Many React jobs ask for TypeScript, because it catches many bugs early and makes big projects easier to understand. This lesson shows the parts you need for React, with plain language.
Why use TypeScript?

items: It finds **typos and wrong values** as you type, such as `user.nmae` or passing a string where a number is needed.
It gives **better auto-complete** in your editor, because it knows the shape of your data.
It works as **living documentation**: you can see what props a component needs without opening it.
It makes **changing code safer**, because the editor shows every place that must change.

content.text: The price is a little extra writing and a short time to learn. TypeScript is removed when your app is built, so the browser still runs plain JavaScript. It does not make code run faster or slower.
Start a TypeScript project

npm create vite@latest my-ts-app -- --template react-ts
cd my-ts-app
npm install
npm run dev
Files now end in `.ts` (plain code) and `.tsx` (code with JSX). Use `.tsx` for components.
The basic types
TypeScript can often **guess** a type, so you do not always write it. `const age = 24` is already known to be a number. Write types where TypeScript cannot guess, such as function parameters.
Describing objects: type and interface

`interface` is almost the same and you will see both. A simple rule: use `type` or `interface` consistently in your project. The union of allowed words, like `'admin' | 'editor'`, is very useful for statuses and options.
Typing props
Now the editor tells you exactly which props a component needs and what type each should be, with no need to open the file.
For components that take `children`, use `ReactNode`:
Typing state
`useState` often guesses the type from the first value. When the first value does not show the full type, tell it with angle brackets (a **generic**):

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);                  // number, guessed
const [name, setName] = useState('');                   // string, guessed

const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);    // a User, or nothing yet
const [items, setItems] = useState<string[]>([]);       // an empty list of text
`useState<User | null>(null)` says: this may hold a user or `null`. Now TypeScript makes you check for `null` before using it, which prevents the very common error “cannot read property of null”:

if (!user) return

Loading...

; return

{user.name}

; // safe: TypeScript knows user is a User here
Typing events

You do not have to remember these names. If you write the handler **inline**, TypeScript knows the type already: `onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)}`. You only need a name when you write the handler as a separate function. Your editor will tell you the right one when you hover over the prop.
Typing refs
Typing API data
Describe what you expect from the server, then use that type when you fetch:

A type is only a promise you make to the editor. TypeScript **cannot check what the server really sends** while the app runs. If the server changes, the type can be wrong. For important data, check it at runtime with a library such as Zod, which can also create the type for you.
Typing context and custom hooks

The `T` in `useLocalStorage<T>` is a **generic**: a placeholder for any type. `useLocalStorage('count', 0)` makes `T` a number, and `useLocalStorage('user', { name: '' })` makes it an object. One hook, many types, all checked.
Useful tools to know

items: **`Partial<User>`** makes all fields optional. Useful for updates.
**`Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>`** keeps only some fields, and **`Omit<User, 'email'>`** removes some.
**`Record<string, number>`** is an object with text keys and number values.
**`as const`** makes a value read-only and exact.
**`unknown`** is a safe version of `any`. It forces you to check the type before using it.

content.text: Avoid any

The type `any` turns off checking for that value. It is tempting when a type is hard, but each `any` removes the safety you came for. Use `unknown` and narrow it, or write a simple type. Turn on `strict` mode in `tsconfig.json` (Vite does it for you), so TypeScript is as helpful as possible.
Reading TypeScript errors

Errors can look long. Read the **last line** first, because it states the real difference, and read **where** (file and line). Hover the red line in your editor for a clearer explanation. Most errors in the first weeks are: a value that might be `null`, a missing prop, a wrong type in a prop, or a typo in a field name. All are good catches.
Common mistakes

items: Using `any` to make errors go away.
Typing `useState([])` with no type, which makes the list `never[]`. Write `useState<string[]>([])`.
Forgetting that data from the network is not checked at runtime.
Casting with `as` to silence an error, hiding a real problem.
Not enabling strict mode.

content.text: A tiny TypeScript story

Here is why people like TypeScript, in a small story. A teammate renames the field `name` to `fullName` in the `User` type. In plain JavaScript, nothing tells you which of your thirty components used `user.name`. Some of them silently show `undefined` on the page, and you only find out when a visitor complains. In TypeScript, the moment the type changes, the editor underlines every place that still says `user.name`. You fix them in a few minutes, and nothing reaches your visitors.

That is the main benefit: **mistakes show up while you write, not after you publish**. It is a safety net for changing code, and the bigger the project, the more it helps. For a tiny practice app you may not need it, and that is fine. Many people learn React first and add TypeScript in the next project.
How to move from JavaScript step by step

items: Start a new project with the `react-ts` template, and write only simple types at first: props, and state with a generic.
Let TypeScript guess types where it can, and write types for function parameters and data from the network.
Read each error calmly. They are hints about real mistakes.
Add more advanced types, such as generics and utility types, only when you need them.

content.text: Your task

items: Create a Vite React TypeScript project and make a `Button` component with typed props, including a `variant` union.
Create a `User` type, and a `UserCard` component that takes a `user` prop. Try passing a wrong field and read the error.
Fetch posts from the sample API and type the result with a `Post` type.
Make a generic `useLocalStorage<T>` hook and use it with a string and with an object.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The editor shows red lines when you pass a wrong prop, and the error message makes sense.
Auto-complete shows the fields of your `User` type.
`npm run build` runs with no TypeScript errors.

content.text: Summary

items: TypeScript adds types to JavaScript and finds mistakes in your editor before you run the app.
Type props with `type` or `interface`, state with `useState<Type>()`, and events with `ChangeEvent` and similar types.
Use unions for fixed options, `?` for optional fields, and generics for reusable hooks.
Avoid `any`, check network data at runtime, and keep strict mode on.

faqs.q: Do I need TypeScript to use React?
faqs.a: No. React works with plain JavaScript. TypeScript is popular in teams and jobs because it catches many mistakes early.

faqs.q: Should I learn JavaScript before TypeScript?
faqs.a: Yes. TypeScript is JavaScript plus types, so you need the JavaScript basics first.

faqs.q: What does useState<User | null>(null) mean?
faqs.a: The state can hold a User object or null. TypeScript then makes you check for null before using it.

faqs.q: Does TypeScript run in the browser?
faqs.a: No. It is turned into plain JavaScript when you build the app. The browser never sees the types.
